articles.title: The Socialist Electoral Project Still Hasn’t Hit Its Ceiling
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Last night was a sobering one for the Left. After months of exhilarating victories, including Abdul El-Sayed’s stunning Michigan Senate primary win just last week, the Left’s hopes for another high-profile Midwest triumph crashed in Wisconsin, where socialist gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong saw her double-digit polling lead evaporate into a 0.5 point defeat to the Democratic establishment’s centrist choice, David Crowley. That result is already being used to create the impression that this was a wholesale rejection of socialists up and down the ballot, which is not the case. Five of eight candidates endorsed by Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapters in Wisconsin and Minnesota won their races last night, while one more has advanced without a primary, and a further five of seven DSA-backed candidates are moving on to the general election in Connecticut and Vermont. And one of those losing DSA-backed candidates lost to another, non-DSA-endorsed socialist. But there is no doubt Hong’s race was by far the most coveted prize for the Left last night and the most important electoral test for socialists in particular, given it was a statewide race in the Midwest and that unlike the victorious El-Sayed in Michigan, Hong actually identifies as a socialist. What explains such a bitter, if narrow, defeat only one week after the broad Left was riding high in a neighboring state? Was it the money? If Michigan proved that big money can be overcome, Wisconsin is a reminder that it still often wins out. Pro-Hong forces were massively outspent , their less than half a million dollars on ad spending dwarfed by the $4 million spent by the pro-Crowley camp, a significant chunk of which went toward an attack ad in the home stretch casting Hong as a risky candidate in the general election. Weeks before the election, 45 percent of voters were undecided, and there is ample anecdotal evidence that they were swayed by messaging that cast doubt on Hong’s ability to appeal to a wider electorate in the general. “Fear won out last night, by a narrow margin,” says socialist State Assembly Member Ryan Clancy, who also won reelection last night to his third term. “It was the idea from the beginning, to make a campaign based on character assassination and focused on the specter of electability, instead of on what Wisconsin needs after a decade of Republican control.” Was it the campaign’s own unforced errors? Hong didn’t go negative against her opponents, even as they turned to attacking her and fearmongering about her old tweets. She was also the only candidate to not spend a single dollar on traditional TV and focus instead on streaming services and other digital ads, a deliberate strategy her campaign manager boasted about on the eve of the election. Hong herself seemed to recognize that mistakes had been made, reportedly planning to replace campaign staff with more experienced operatives if she had won the race. Was it Hong’s own vulnerabilities as a candidate? Hong was hammered in the final weeks over old “ woke ” tweets expressing support for abolishing the police, calling to “cancel Thanksgiving” and other beloved holidays, and discussing race in alienating ways that reflected the prevailing progressive style of the era but that have aged poorly now — particularly on public safety, as some socialists are beginning to argue for a “ carceral minimalism ” framework rather than “abolishing” prison or police. Hong attempted to do as other socialist candidates like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani have done and parry these and other attacks by making explicit that she was charting a new course on criminal justice and public safety. But she was not as successful in persuading skeptical voters on it. Was it the reluctance of leading socialist figures like Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to lend their endorsement to Hong? They and a parade of other high-profile socialist candidates who had a week earlier rallied with El-Sayed declined to show up for Hong, reportedly because of private doubts about her effectiveness as a candidate. Opinion in the cold light of day is split between whether this could have moved the needle just enough to get Hong the few thousand more votes she needed, or whether Hong’s defeat showed socialist officials were right to stay away. This will likely be a matter of intense debate for some time. Whatever the case, the months ahead should be a period of self-reflection for the Left if it wants to build off Hong’s surprisingly strong campaign and take advantage of an appetite that clearly exists among the state’s Democratic electorate for a robust left-wing politics. Hong’s defeat won’t be the only disappointment in Wisconsin that socialists will have to reflect on. Former Catholic priest David Liners, who had been endorsed by Hong, Clancy, and Wisconsin Electoral Socialists — an organization founded two years ago to support socialist candidates for public office — fell short last night in his state assembly bid. So did the DSA-endorsed socialist running for Hong’s state assembly seat, Juliana Bennett . But while this might be a setback for perceptions of the power of DSA’s ground game, it is not necessarily one for the movement as a whole: the candidate who beat her, Madison Common Council Member Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, is also a socialist and will become the first openly transgender person to serve in Wisconsin’s state legislature if she wins in the general. Meanwhile, in the primary to see who would try to flip the purple Third Congressional District, former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge — not a socialist but endorsed by the local DSA chapter — lost to her more centrist opponent, Rebecca Cooke, in another race that shows that Sanders and the movement he inspired don’t always overlap. Sanders had chosen Cooke, a former Democratic fundraiser who now works as a restaurant server, as his only Wisconsin endorsee this cycle, even though she dragged her feet on backing a data center moratorium and has waffled on Medicare for All. This string of losses in Wisconsin will be a bitter pill to swallow for socialists in and beyond the state. But it should also be kept in perspective. For one, Clancy tells me that the Wisconsin Legislative Socialist Caucus is set to expand from its current four members in the next legislative session, even with the loss of Hong who joined two years ago, though he can’t disclose specific names of new members just yet. Looking more broadly, the fact that Hong, a three-term socialist state assembly member, even got as far as she did is a fairly remarkable development for the Left. The socialist caucus in Wisconsin’s legislature did not even exist four years ago, and the last time one did was nearly ninety years before that. This result means that in the space of a few years, socialists have gone from having no representation in the state legislature, to just two assembly members, to coming within less than half a percentage point of taking the Democratic nomination for governor. While the Hong defeat is a setback in the short term, from a wider lens, her campaign is the product of rapid socialist growth that no centrist Democrat in the state will be looking at with carefree eyes. Beyond the Dairy State Looking beyond Wisconsin, things were brighter for the Left. The most high-profile victory was Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan’s win over the centrist, ex-medical-device-industry-executive Angie Craig in neighboring Minnesota’s Senate primary, the only other endorsement Sanders made for this set of primaries. While Flanagan is not a socialist, she had a better, albeit somewhat mixed , record on Israel and Palestine than Craig, and some of her policy commitments overlap with those of socialists, like her support of Medicare for All. In the end, Craig’s vote for Trump’s turbocharged immigration crackdown that wreaked death and havoc in Minnesota proved to be her undoing. In terms of DSA-backed candidates, Omar Fateh, who narrowly lost the Minneapolis mayor’s race to the centrist incumbent last year, cruised to reelection in the Minnesota State Senate, and two other DSA-endorsed incumbents — Liish Kozlowski in the state house and Jen McEwen in the state senate — have moved on to the general election without contest. It wasn’t just incumbents. Kris Eilers, running on a platform of environmental protection and resisting corporate influence, won the most votes in the three-way race for St Louis County Commissioner in the First District and will face the second-most vote getter and incumbent in the seat come November. Meanwhile, Christin Crabtree, backed by DSA’s Twin Cities chapter, won a seat to Minneapolis’s school board. Crabtree, a public-school teacher and anti–Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activist during the Trump administration’s deadly Operation Metro Surge earlier this year, won on the back of a door-knocking campaign that saw local DSA members pair campaigning for Crabtree with organizing against the federal immigration crackdown, according to Twin Cities DSA Communications Coordinator Lena Pak. Meanwhile, progressive Matthew Little overcame an avalanche of more than $3 million worth of pro-Israel lobby spending to win the race for Craig’s seat in Congress by 17 points. That not only adds yet another “Squad”-adjacent and pro-Palestine voice in Congress but marks the latest expensive failure for the pro-Israel lobby’s interference in Democratic primary elections, one week after after flushing away $30 million to lose the Senate race in Michigan. The Midwest wasn’t the only region that saw primary elections last night, nor the only place where socialists won less high-profile races. Maybe most notable is Maryam Khan, the two-term state representative who has now won the primary to become the first ever Muslim state senator in Connecticut history. After outreach from Connecticut DSA, who were impressed with her progressive record in the legislature — including her opposition to charter schools, support for abolishing ICE, and strong pro-Palestine position — and with the New York races demystifying socialism for the broader public, Khan became a dues-paying DSA member and won the chapter’s endorsement earlier this year. That win was somewhat offset by the defeat of the state house campaign of socialist Justin Farmer, who previously served six years on the Hamden town council. Meanwhile, in Vermont, socialist Tanya Vyhovsky won reelection to the state senate, while two nonincumbent socialists are heading to safe seats in the general election. One, Burlington’s Jeffrey Peterson, effectively took the nomination uncontested for the district currently held by the outgoing state house speaker, while another, school district librarian Matt Gile, won the state house primary for Chittenden’s Twenty-First District with 38 percent of the vote. Two others — Nick Gauthier in Connecticut and Alexander Bobella in Vermont — have moved onto the general election for state legislature seats with no primary. Still Room to Go Tuesday’s result was a contradiction: at once a bitter, disappointing defeat for socialists that shows the movement still has a way to go to broaden its appeal to voters and to ease the anxieties of electability-focused Democratic voters; and a marker of how far and rapidly the movement has come at the electoral level, in a state where socialists have been invisible for more than half a century and only recently begun to reshore their numbers, no less. Hong’s defeat was a setback for the Left. But whatever her political future, Hong’s campaign will be remembered for potentially opening the door to a new era of politics for Wisconsin and the Left more broadly — if the Left plays its hand correctly. Hong’s razor-thin losing margin, some of the details specific to her race, and the continuing, steady accumulation of downballot socialist victories across both the Midwest and other parts of the country suggest that socialists have not hit a wall quite yet. Rather, if they are willing to honestly assess what went wrong, there is still room to go before they touch the ceiling.

articles.title: When Elites Scheme Behind Closed Doors
articles.author: Andrew Hartman
articles.content: In the recent Democratic primary in Missouri’s first congressional district, which includes all of St Louis and much of northern St Louis County, including Ferguson, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC)–funded incumbent Wesley Bell bucked national trends. Whereas AIPAC support has become an albatross for many candidates running in Democratic primaries, Bell easily defeated former congresswoman and Israel critic Cori Bush. Although the money AIPAC funneled into the primary indicates Middle East politics played an outsize role in the struggle to control a black-majority Missouri district, deeply rooted local concerns seemed weightier. This is not surprising: the political careers of both Bell and Bush began in 2014 with the protests that engulfed Ferguson in response to the police murder of Michael Brown. Bush supporters, thus, not only brought attention to Bell’s ties to AIPAC, but also to his Deputy Chief of Staff Jordan Blase’s controversial past as a Veiled Prophet debutante. As a local activist said on Instagram, after spotting an album of photos on Blase’s Facebook page dedicated to the annual Veiled Prophet Ball, Blase and her family “have been attending their white supremacist ball for decades.” What in the hell is a “Veiled Prophet,” you might ask? And why is Blase’s history with it controversial (though not controversial enough to tilt the race in favor of Bush)? For answers to these questions and many more about the history of St Louis elite society, we turn to Devin Thomas O’Shea’s fascinating new book, The Veiled Prophet: Secret Societies, White Supremacy, and the Struggle for St Louis . Reconstruction and the Great Railroad Strike The Veiled Prophet Society, a purportedly secret organization with a highly exclusive membership that hosts an annual parade and a debutante ball, was founded in 1877 for the explicit purpose of shielding the local bourgeoisie from an increasingly militant proletariat. It was no coincidence that the Veiled Prophet Society was created in the smoldering aftermath of the Great Railroad Strikes of 1877, or that it was established in St Louis, where workers not only walked off the job but also organized to take control of the city. The Veiled Prophet Society was formed to destroy the specter of working-class solidarity that momentarily sprang to life in what contemporaries called the St Louis Commune, comparing it to the more famous 1871 Paris Commune. The St Louis Commune, led by the short-lived Workingmen’s Party of the United States (WPUS) — the first Marxist party in the United States — briefly took power in East St Louis, the section of the city on the east side of the Mississippi and a rail hub and industrial loading dock. The Great Railroad Strike, which began in West Virginia and fanned out across multiple states, disrupting the nation’s circulation of goods, was a violent affair. In response to workers burning down railroad facilities, the companies, enlisting private militias, local and state police, and federal troops, put down the strike with malice, killing about 150 workers. Unlike strikers elsewhere, St Louis workers refrained from destroying property, since their objective was to expropriate it for their own use. They were successful for about a week, before the forces of capital took back control of the city. The title page for the program of the 1883 Veiled Prophet Festival. To protect their interests in the face of an assertive proletariat, the St Louis bourgeoisie created the ironically named Committee for Public Safety, which, unlike the original French revolutionary committee of the same name, was designed to crush rather than defend hard-won republican rights. “The strike,” O’Shea writes, “was an effort to crown the workers as the masters” of the enormous wealth that flowed through St Louis in the nineteenth century, such abundance owing to the city sitting along the largest inland waterway on the continent, at the crossroads of both the nation’s east–west and north–south frontiers. “The city’s financial interests used racism, and the barrel of a gun, to quash that effort.” The racism of St Louis elites is central to O’Shea’s story. One of the keys to the brief success of the St Louis working class in 1877 was its interracial solidarity. And one of the lasting features of the Veiled Prophet Society, which was formed out of the Committee for Public Safety and has been in existence ever since, has been its white supremacy. The founder of the Veiled Prophet Society, St Louis native Alonzo Slayback, is prima facie evidence of O’Shea’s argument about white supremacy being the establishing principle of the organization. Slayback was an officer in the Confederate Army and a true believer in the cause of the South, slavery. After the United States defeated the Confederacy, Slayback followed notorious Confederate General Jo Shelby south to Mexico City, where they hoped to escape punishment for their treason. A portrait of Alonzo W. Slayback, circa 1882. Shelby, Slayback, and company solicited help from fellow reactionary elite, Emperor Maximilian I, the Austrian archduke reigning over the so-called Second Mexican Empire. As a member of the European ruling class, Maximilian was closely aligned with the potentate of the Second French Empire, Napoleon III (known to posterity as Karl Marx’s object of mockery — in The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte , Marx famously described Napoleon III’s ascension as a farce). The account of defeated Confederates in Mexico City seeking help from a soon-to-be executed European monarch (Maximilian met his death by firing squad in 1867) is one of many stories of unhinged conduct common to the rich, powerful, and reactionary men of the Veiled Prophet Society. Such elite vulgarity will seem familiar to twenty-first-century readers. From Elon Musk’s (alleged) ketamine-induced displays of neurotic Nazism to Peter Thiel’s (confirmed) obsession with the Antichrist, repugnant behavior is a timeless characteristic of rich, powerful, and reactionary men. We can only wish our current oligarchs were, like their Confederate predecessors, on the run, seeking shelter in a foreign capital. Little did Slayback know when he traveled south of the border, that a full pardon awaited him upon his homecoming. (One of the biggest political mistakes in US history is letting those who committed treason in defense of slavery off the hook so easily.) Slayback returned to St Louis in 1866 and started a law practice. He had rejoined an elite class of Americans that by 1877 wished to turn the page on the Civil War and Reconstruction and instead focus its attention on capital accumulation. The ultimate objective of the Veiled Prophet Society was protecting its members’ wealth. Upholding racial hierarchy was a secondary, though interconnected, goal. The Veiled Prophet, the society’s mysterious mascot annually paraded before the St Louis rabble, wears a Ku Klux Klan–inspired mask and robe that double as odes to the Irish poet Thomas Moore’s orientalist tale, Lalla Rookh . The Veiled Prophet was intended to evoke awe of the local elite among the working-class masses who lined the streets of St Louis each year and watched as the wealthy paraded by them. O’Shea describes what motivated Slayback and his fellow elites to concoct such an absurdity: The Veiled Prophet Society would be a Mardi Gras club for white men to parade their power in the streets of St Louis, communicating their message to the proletariat — that Americans are white and civilized and that the rest of the world is barbaric and Black; that the threat of Southern plantation violence was not dead, but lay dormant in everyday life; but most of all, that commerce reigns supreme and should operate freely without checks or restraints. The mascot often stimulated ridicule, even anger, especially among black locals who rejected the parade’s nostalgia for plantation slavery. The Veiled Prophet was frequently the target of various projectiles along the parade route. Yet despite bouts of mostly harmless resistance from local proles, the Veiled Prophet Society was apparently successful in reversing the republicanism that had made its home in St Louis during the Civil War and Reconstruction. Elites overturned a widespread radical sensibility, nicely expressed by Marx’s German ’48er comrade Joseph Weydemeyer, a colonel in the Union Army who was placed in command of forces defending St Louis during the war. In an 1866 essay promoting black suffrage, Weydemeyer argued that, in the struggle against capital, workers needed to join forces “regardless of what ancestry they have to thank for their skin color.” Weydemeyer advocated for the very same multiracial working-class formation that W. E. B. DuBois later mourned in his monumental 1935 book, Black Reconstruction in America . Into the 20th Century In the book’s interregnum of sorts, O’Shea narrates a gripping tale that turns out to be a serious plot twist. On October 13, 1882, Slayback barged into St Louis Post-Dispatch editor John A. Cockerill’s office. The former Confederate general was outraged over the rough treatment the newspaper had been dishing out to his law partner and fellow Veiled Prophet Society member James Broadhead, who was running for local office. An angry Slayback arrived armed and loaded, but Cockerill got the jump on him, shooting and killing him. Convinced the newspaperman had acted in self-defense, local authorities never charged Cockerill with a crime. The founder of the Veiled Prophet Society was pronounced dead at the age of forty-four. But the secret organization did not perish alongside him. The king is dead, long live the king. As The Veiled Prophet Society moves into the twentieth century, we learn about the growing prestige of the group during the era of its close kin, the second Ku Klux Klan, when the “club commanded the attention of presidents, and robber barons like Jay Gould were compelled to attend the ball.” We also learn about the larger history of St Louis and its segregated and easily exploited industrial workforce, part and parcel of ongoing racial violence which at times exploded, such as in a 1917 racial pogrom that left around 150 black residents dead. Resistance to the Veiled Prophet Society was sporadic at best, only truly gaining momentum in the 1930s, a time when the organization was more “severely out of touch” than usual. Until then, the club had acted as a symbol of elite unification and working-class fracture. But in the age of the Congress of Industrial Organizations , when even the normally taboo Communist Party USA experienced rapid growth, it was more difficult for an older, venal bourgeoisie — the exact type that constituted the Veiled Prophet Society — to preserve its hegemonic grip on the political culture. Yet in St Louis, as elsewhere in the United States, the ruling class adjusted to new circumstances. One of the better indicators that the old elite remained dominant, even during the postwar age of high Fordism, was in how it dictated the terms of urban renewal, which was all the rage in postwar American cities. Urban renewal policies transformed St Louis, but not for the better, especially for the black working class. A 1947 portrait of then-adviser to Harry S. Truman, Clark Clifford. Several newly constructed highways carved up the heart of the city, clearing out historically black neighborhoods. A massive housing project, Pruitt-Igoe, opened its doors in 1954 to thousands of displaced and impoverished residents, only to be demolished after two decades of severe neglect. None of which is to say that a public housing project is an inherently bad idea. But public goods must be nurtured if they are to be, well, good . Meanwhile, as Pruitt-Igoe was starved to death, the Veiled Prophet Society resumed celebrating high society, emphasizing its annual ball, where its luckiest daughters were honored as brides of the Veiled Prophet. Another sign that the Veiled Prophet Society, an inherently reactionary entity, retained its mojo even at the high point of American liberalism was when President Harry Truman, a Missouri man, brought a Veiled Prophet contingent with him to Washington, DC. Most notable among them was Clark Clifford, who helped establish the Central Intelligence Agency in 1947. Clifford went on to serve in several Democratic administrations, including briefly as Lyndon B. Johnson’s secretary of defense. Another Veiled Prophet Society member, Tom Dooley, operated as a spy in Southeast Asia prior to the Vietnam War. Dooley gained notoriety as author of the anti-communist screed Deliver Us from Evil , an ostensible dismantling of Ho Chi Minh that was in fact a total fabrication. During the Cold War, the Veiled Prophet Society had joined what C. Wright Mills labeled “the power elite,” the overlapping network of government, business, and military brokers who ruled the United States and, by extension, much of the world. Does the Ruling Class Need Secret Societies? The Veiled Prophet Society is a fun and informative book, especially for sickos like me who never tire of reading about the American class struggle, even though the struggle almost never tilts in favor of the working class. But O’Shea’s overarching analysis is too heavily reliant on assuming the historical agency of the Veiled Prophet Society. The not-so-secret club is a window onto elite capitalist society and how it operates to protect its interests. It is not a mechanism, or at least not the mechanism, for defending modern capitalist hierarchy. O’Shea’s book is excellent in describing the strange manifestations of the American class struggle from the perspective of the elites who had a lot to gain from maintaining capitalist arrangements. But the existence of a secret society itself, even one so embedded in a specific location, is not a smoking gun. There is no conspiracy other than the grand conspiracy of capitalism that has been known to us since Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote about the “new conditions of oppression” in The Communist Manifesto . O’Shea’s skill in narrating a tale, alongside his somewhat upside-down analysis, is evident in his half-hearted conjecture that the Veiled Prophet Society was possibly responsible for the assassination of Martin Luther King, Jr — a possibility that was investigated by the House Select Committee on Assassinations in the late 1970s and dismissed. O’Shea begrudgingly admits that the evidence connecting the club to the murderer, James Earl Ray, who spent a significant amount of time in St Louis and was born nearby, is at best speculative. But he also implies that the connection is true in the way good fiction is true. “It makes sense,” he writes, “that a narrative developed around King and the Prophet. One is royalty of the African American struggle, the other is the monarch of the cut-throat white business classes; two entities at war with one another for the soul of America.” The civil rights movement in St Louis forced the Veiled Prophet Society on its heels with a campaign of constant harassment. The elite club responded by shutting down its parade, which had become an easy target of backlash, and by instead hosting an annual fair under the shadow of the Gateway Arch. Anodyne music acts, generic food vendors, and plenty of Budweiser replaced the Veiled Prophet and its racist baggage. Eventually organizers even ditched the Veiled Prophet Society moniker, as the club tried to hide its controversial identity as sponsor of the fair. The Veiled Prophet Society’s efforts to clean up its image also led to incremental efforts to diversify its membership. The first black member was admitted to Alonzo Slayback’s club in the early 1980s. By 2014, the year of the Ferguson uprising, the Veiled Prophet Society was a shell of its former self. And yet the elite are in firm control of St Louis and almost every other American city. The Left is doing better than it has in a while, but capitalism is far from threatened. Secret societies and similar such elite clubs are hardly necessary for continued ruling class domination. One question that O’Shea’s book raises: Were they ever?

articles.title: The Human Cost of Google’s AI Expansion
articles.author: Anuj Behal
articles.content: For nearly six months, Relli Ramakrishna has not made the daily walk to the small farm where she spent most of her life cultivating cashews, mangoes, and seasonal vegetables. Now her mornings pass in a quiet repetition of boredom. She stays at home, attending to chores that end long before the day does. “There is nothing left for me to do,” she says. “The farm was my work. It was where I spent my time.” The land in Tarluvada, a village on the outskirts of Visakhapatnam in the southern Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, was acquired as part of Google’s ambitious plan to build a large data center across three sites , a project the government has championed as the cornerstone of India’s artificial intelligence ambitions. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, plans to invest $15 billion over the next five years to build the data center, its largest outside the United States. It will be linked to Singapore, South Africa, Australia, and the US through a network of sub-sea and terrestrial fiber optic cables. For families such as Relli’s, however, the arrival of AI has begun with the disappearance of the land beneath their feet. The AI Land Grab Relli, who is in her late sixties, belongs to a Dalit community — a group historically discriminated against under India’s caste system and still, by most measures, India’s most land-poor community. Between 58 and 71 percent of rural Dalit households are landless. In the 1970s, the Andhra Pradesh government allotted small parcels of land to Relli’s family and fifty others in Tarluvada — two acres each for cultivation, along with additional plots for housing. “Before this land, we survived on the goodwill of dominant-caste landowners we worked for,” Relli says. “Some days we weren’t paid at all — just given rice porridge for a day’s labor.” The allotted land was rocky, uneven, and barely fit for cultivation, she says. Over the years, her family leveled the ground, improved the soil, and planted cashew and mango trees, turning it into a dependable source of income. “We made it fertile with our blood and sweat,” says Relli. The farm earned her family nearly 100,000 rupees ($1,048) a year — modest by most standards but enough to transform their lives. “This land lets us stand on our own,” she says. The Tarluvada site is now part of the land the state government has acquired for Google’s data center. The fifty-one families were offered eight million rupees ($83,848) — 4 million rupees for each acre — along with a promise of land equivalent to one-fifth of their acquired holding elsewhere, though where remains unclear. The compensation has largely been distributed, but residents say they had little warning of what was happening. “No one asked us if we wanted to leave,” says Pyla Kondamma, a farmer and former head of the village council. “They just told us to hand the land over. This is our way of life — why should the decision about whether to give it up not be ours?” The state has described the payout as generous, but Dr E. A. S. Sarma, a former secretary in India’s power ministry who has opposed the project, argues that the state has effectively subsidized Google’s investment by acquiring land at prices far below its market value. “The people who are subsidizing this project are Dalit and small landholding families,” he says. “They are being paid a fraction of what the land is actually worth.” Earthwork, including land clearance and site grading, is underway at Google’s proposed data center site near Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh. Residents and activists say police surveillance around the site has intensified as construction has accelerated. (Anuj Behal / Jacobin ) For many families, the compensation offers a chance to patch over years of deprivation. Some are expanding single-story homes into two- and three-story concrete buildings. Others are replacing aging brick structures with new houses. “The land is gone now. We cannot bring it back. At least this money gives us a chance to build a proper house on the land that remains,” says resident P. Bangarama, sixty. Compensation Does Not Buy Consent The construction boom, however, should not be mistaken for acceptance of the acquisition, says Sushmita Pati, a political scientist at the National Law School of India University. Compensation, she says, often produces two parallel realities: the grief of losing land that embodies “livelihood, identity and emotional attachment,” alongside the opportunity to fulfil long-deferred aspirations through an unusually large lump-sum payment. “People don’t give up land out of happiness,” she says. “Those two realities can exist simultaneously.” For Dalit families in particular, Pati says, compensation may finally enable investments that had remained out of reach for generations, but it does not erase the loss of agricultural land. Rather, she says, it reflects how communities negotiate dispossession — making pragmatic decisions about the resources they have left while continuing to mourn what they have lost. Not everyone is ready to build. Shankar Chandala, twenty-nine, remains undecided about whether to invest in a new home amid the uncertainty of what the data center might bring. “What will these data centers leave us with?” he asks. “They will need enormous amounts of water and electricity. What if there isn’t enough water in the future? What if, a few years from now, they want to expand again, and we’re asked to give up our homes the way we gave up our fields?” New homes are rising across Tarluvada village after many families received compensation for land acquired for Google’s proposed data center. (Anuj Behal / Jacobin ) Chandala says he has spent months reading about such “hyperscale” data centers and the strain they can place on water, electricity, and the environment. “I always dreamed of building my own house here,” he says. “But a dream house is one where I don’t have to worry about water, pollution, or losing my home again. I’m not sure I can build that here anymore.” His worry tracks with what is publicly known about the industry: a large data center can draw up to five million gallons of water a day at full operation — roughly the daily water use of a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. Evading Public Review Google did not respond to Jacobin ’s questions about the data center’s expected water and electricity consumption, nor has it publicly disclosed those figures. For many residents of Visakhapatnam, water is already rationed. Households receive piped supply for only a few hours each day, while many informal settlements depend largely on private water tankers. As of April 2026, Visakhapatnam had Andhra Pradesh’s lowest groundwater reserves available for use. To position Visakhapatnam at the center of India’s AI ambitions, the Andhra Pradesh government has assembled an incentive package worth an estimated 220 billion rupees (about $21 million ), offering Google’s project concessional land, tax waivers, subsidized electricity, and expedited clearances. But environmental groups say the government’s drive to accelerate the project has come at the expense of due process and ecological scrutiny. Despite their vast demand for land, water, and electricity, data centers are regulated as conventional construction projects under India’s environmental clearance regime, placing them under a state-level appraisal process rather than the more stringent central review, which requires public consultation. The regulatory distinction has had tangible consequences, with two of Google’s three proposed sites, covering about 440 acres, securing state environmental clearance in about ten days . One of the sites is less than a mile from Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary, an ecologically sensitive forest that supports wildlife including the Indian leopard. A statue of Dr B. R. Ambedkar in Tarluvada’s Dalit colony. Across India, Ambedkar’s image is a familiar presence in Dalit settlements, symbolizing dignity, equality, and the assertion of constitutional rights. (Anuj Behal / Jacobin ) V. S. Krishna, an activist with the NGO Human Rights Forum , says the ongoing hill-cutting and forest clearance could disrupt the natural drainage that feeds the local Mudasarlova Reservoir, threatening both the wildlife corridor linking the sanctuary with the adjoining Kailasagiri forest and water supplies to much of Visakhapatnam. At the third site, spanning the villages of Adavivaram and Mudasarlova, the Human Rights Forum alleges that forest land was cleared and hill-cutting had already begun before the project received environmental clearance. “The clearance process was reduced to a fait accompli,” says Krishna. The Andhra Pradesh State Environment Impact Assessment Authority later granted clearance for the site. Hungry for Power Energy is another flash point. A data center of this scale could require as much electricity as a midsize city, raising concerns about the strain it could place on Andhra Pradesh’s power grid. Although Google has committed to powering the facility with renewable energy, state officials have acknowledged that renewable energy alone cannot reliably meet its demands, and that additional coal-fired generation will be required to ensure around-the-clock supply. “Data centers don’t eliminate pollution by buying renewable electricity,” Krishna says. “If the grid still relies on coal to guarantee uninterrupted power, the environmental and health burden is simply displaced to communities living around coal-fired power plants. Someone else ends up paying the price.” With construction advancing and earthmovers reshaping the landscape, many residents acknowledge that stopping the project may no longer be realistic. Instead, the struggle has shifted toward demanding transparency over its environmental impacts, stronger safeguards, and a greater share of its promised benefits. With villagers, the Human Rights Forum has filed objections, organized public meetings, documented construction activities, and launched a petition seeking the disclosure of the project’s water and electricity requirements. Residents in Tarluvada say the space for dissent has narrowed as the project has gathered pace. Several people say police presence intensified around the village during the inauguration of the project in April by the chief minister of the state, N. Chandrababu Naidu , discouraging public protest. The pressure has extended online. In recent months, the Human Rights Forum reported that its Instagram posts documenting the project were being restricted , and the Environmental Reporting Collective, a journalist network, says an investigative video examining the impact of the data center on Dalit land has been blocked in India. Meanwhile, Google’s servers are expected to come online in 2028. Chandala says he is still trying to imagine what his future will look like by then. “Will we get the land the government promised us to cultivate?” he asks. “Or will we become landless Dalits again?”

articles.title: Five Takeaways From Francesca Hong’s Near-Win in Wisconsin
articles.author: Paul Heideman
articles.content: Francesca Hong, the democratic socialist running in the Democratic primary for the Wisconsin governor’s race, lost last night in an extremely close election. She came within half a percentage point of beating David Crowley, the executive of Milwaukee County. Preelection polling showed Hong with a commanding lead, and many assumed she would coast to victory. As such, her result is being spun as a hard defeat for the socialist left. The truth is more complicated. Hong accomplished a great deal in her campaign, and even her loss contains valuable lessons for future attempts. 1. Horse-Race Polling Warps the Narrative Perhaps the biggest lesson from this race is that a focus on the horse-race polling makes for bad politics. Since serious polling for this race began, Hong held a solid lead. She led current Lieutenant Governor Sara Rodriguez by 10 points even before Rodriguez had to drop out because of campaign finance mishaps. Crowley, who ultimately won, hadn’t come within 20 points of Hong since March. Because of this, Hong’s victory was widely viewed as all but inevitable. But the polls were wrong. Turnout was up significantly from the last statewide Democratic primary in 2022. And large numbers of voters were clearly waiting to make up their minds. Hong’s lead in the polls lent itself to a narrative of her as a prohibitive favorite. This was clearly a mistake. And it obscures how far the campaign came. When Hong launched her campaign back in September of last year, she described herself as a wild card in the race and was largely treated as a fringe candidate. The vast majority of voters in the state had never heard of her. She was a state assembly member (a part-time position in Wisconsin), and worked in restaurants. But through dedicated campaigning across the state, Hong built up a real profile and won the trust of hundreds of thousands of voters. Coming within half a percent of victory from such a starting point is an objectively impressive achievement. The Democratic establishment in Wisconsin can hardly be thrilled that it was only able to defeat a novice candidate like Hong by the skin of its teeth. But the focus on polling obscures all of this. 2. Subcultural Leftism Hurts Socialists Hong accomplished a tremendous amount in this race. But it is impossible to avoid the conclusion that she could have accomplished much more if she hadn’t had to carry the load of past statements she made exemplifying insular leftist subcultures. A post she had made in 2020 calling for scrapping Thanksgiving for “celebrating colonialism” and “a time that’s incredibly painful for many people in our communities” received a great deal of attention in the last weeks of the race, for example. So did her endorsement of abolishing the police, a slogan I’ve recently argued is a barrier to left success and desperately needed criminal justice reform. And while it’s unlikely that many Democratic primary voters decided not to endorse Hong because they were afraid of being deprived of turkey in November, the sheer number of statements Hong had to walk back in the last few weeks convinced many voters that she would have a hard time defeating the Republican Tom Tiffany in the general election. In a race with margins this tight, it’s at least plausible that all this cost her the race. Hong isn’t the only socialist who got on board with self-marginalizing politics during the “Great Awokening” of the early 2020s. Zohran Mamdani also embraced defunding the police. But by frankly repudiating his earlier position in the campaign and maintaining iron discipline in his focus on affordability in all campaign appearances, he was able to convince voters that he really had changed his positions. Hong’s disavowals, coming out late in the race and made far less forcefully, were not as impactful. For candidates who are freighted with this kind of baggage, extraordinary message discipline is necessary. 3. Socialists Need to Be Able to Make the Case They’ll Defeat Republicans This leads directly into the next point. It should have been clear after Joe Biden’s victory over Bernie Sanders in 2020 that the ability to defeat Republicans in general elections is nonnegotiable for Democratic primary voters. In places like New York City, where the GOP runs a local mascot like Curtis Sliwa for mayor rather than an actual candidate, this is less of a concern. But in a state like Wisconsin, where voters remember the devastation wrought by eight years of Scott Walker’s austerity-crazed, viciously antiunion Republican administration, Democratic primary voters were unwilling to take a chance with someone they viewed as less likely to win the general election. Socialist candidates need to embrace the work of making this case, and need to campaign in a way that demonstrates to voters that we take beating Republicans every bit as seriously as they do. 4. Campaign on What Matters to Voters Hong achieved as much as she did in this race because of her focus on what mattered to voters. She campaigned on free public childcare, taxing the rich, and instituting a one-year moratorium on data center construction. These issues resonated deeply with voters and convinced thousands and thousands to support a candidate they had not even heard of when the race began. To appreciate the way her policies made Hong stand out, compare her plan for free public childcare with Lieutenant Governor Sara Rodriguez’s childcare plan. Rodriguez proposed a means-tested program that would cap childcare expenses at 7 percent of annual income. Given a choice between the two policies, it’s not hard to see why so many voters preferred Hong. Similarly, data centers are deeply unpopular in Wisconsin, and Hong was the only candidate to come out for a moratorium on their construction. Simple, clear policies like these are a strong foundation for outsider candidates. 5. The Space for Socialist Politics, Even Outside of Major Cities Like New York, Is Massive After Zohran Mamdani won the New York City mayoral race in 2025, a common refrain from the pundit choir was that Mamdani’s approach could work in big cities like New York or Chicago but stood no chance in purple states. Hong showed that even in Wisconsin, there is a huge appetite for a break from politics as usual. Her campaign began much like Mamdani’s, with virtually no funding, support, or media visibility. But through hard campaigning across the state, Hong built up a profile, at the same time that the nonsocialist Democrats in the race all failed to inspire much excitement. Much of the commentariat would like to declare that Hong’s loss shows the ceiling on democratic socialist politics in purple states. But given Hong’s burden of subcultural leftism and the reported disorganization of her campaign, it would be more apt to conclude that a more disciplined candidate and campaign with the same platform could have achieved much more. Hong’s campaign both showed the potential that exists for the socialist left in purple states and what we need to do to reach it.

articles.title: John Deere Is Testing Its Workers’ Resolve
articles.author: Jane Slaughter
articles.content: The agricultural machinery maker John Deere tested the mettle of the United Auto Workers (UAW) this summer, probing for softness as the union heads into a leadership election this month. After fits and starts the union essentially told Deere to stick it. As promised, though, members will vote on Deere’s proposal on August 23. Deere wants to extend its six-year contract to eight years. The current pact for ten thousand workers at nine Midwestern plants expires October 31, 2027 — six months before the union’s deals with the Big 3 automakers are up on May 1, 2028 . In 2021, Deere workers struck for thirty-four days, gaining national press. They voted down two offers before winning a 20 percent pay boost over six years, a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), and three lump sums. Jake Lane, education chair at UAW Local 450 in Des Moines, Iowa, told Labor Notes , “Everybody is still pretty proud of our strike.” Another veteran of that winning battle said the company was “mad as f-ck about the 2021 strike still.” “They’re trying to feel how unstable the union is when it comes to who wants what out of a contract,” said Pete Schaefer, from the Harvester Works in East Moline, Illinois. “They’re definitely up to something. The majority of us here understand that.” Deere’s extension would be largely status quo: continue the contract’s remaining annual 4 percent raises, pay a $3,000 signing bonus, and move a 3 percent lump sum scheduled for this fall to fall 2028. Health insurance would be unchanged. Deere builds tractors, combines, cotton pickers, and other high-ticket farm equipment. Its sales are tied to agricultural corporations’ ability to buy. With its proposal, the company claimed to have workers’ interests at heart. Citing “lower commodity prices, higher interest rates and market volatility” that are reducing demand, Deere argued that a contract extension would “protect what our employees already have.” Floored as the Next Guy After weeks of a lack of shared information that frustrated rank-and-file members, the UAW International and the Deere Council, made up of local union leaders, told Deere its unilateral offer was a nonstarter and demanded bargaining instead. Deere initially contacted the UAW Agricultural Implements Department on June 10, right before the union’s convention. On July 6, local union officers met with the UAW vice president in charge of the Agricultural Implements Department, Laura Dickerson, and heard the news. Local 838 President Tim Cummings in Waterloo, Iowa, publicized Deere’s proposal to his members online, writing, “I was just as floored as the next guy.” On July 29, the union’s Deere Council resolved to make a counteroffer. Dickerson’s July 31 statement pointed out: John Deere is asking to change a collective bargaining agreement that both sides already negotiated and signed. When a company comes back to rewrite the deal, it is asking for something. That is bargaining. Deere does not get to ask the union for a favor while acting like the rules of bargaining suddenly do not apply. The union’s counteroffer was substantially richer than Deere’s: 5 percent pay raises instead of 4 percent, two 3 percent lump sums instead of one, roll the cost-of-living adjustment into the base wage off of which everything else is calculated, a $2,000 contribution to retirement accounts for each year of service, and, perhaps most irksome to the company, “no more work or product will be outsourced.” Riffing off Deere’s purported concern for workers, Dickerson added, “This would provide the stability John Deere values for its customers and employees.” Deere claimed the UAW’s proposal would cost an extra half-billion dollars and rejected it out of hand, reminding the union of the rule it had tried to lay down at the outset: its offer was the only thing on the table. “We Don’t Forget” Schaefer remembered, “My first contract that I had with the company being 2008, they laid off a lot of us, knowing that they had a high volume of orders coming in. So it’s hard to trust them after we went through that. “The company is gonna look out for the shareholders and people who invest in the company more than the people, the workers,” he added. “It comes down to the worker is always the expendable asset. That’s why a lot of us just don’t think that they’re doing us a favor by offering this extension. That’s like where the mindset is at Harvester. We don’t forget.” Josh Saunders, a steward at Harvester, said, “I would say it was initially very split between yes, no, and on the fence. And the more discussion has gone on and there’s been lots of great points for and against, I feel like more people are leaning towards no.” Why no? “It would be a lot the same as why we voted no and ended up on strike in ’21,” Saunders said. “We want a bigger piece of the pie. Deere puts out billions of dollars in profits every year, and they balk at paying us a little bit more. They do billions of dollars of stock buybacks. We’re the ones that make the money for the company, and then they’re giving it to someone who doesn’t work here.” Deere has stepped up its outsourcing, including to Mexico. Matt from the Davenport, Iowa, plant (who asked to use his first name only) pointed out that a longer contract meant more time for the company to move work unhindered: “After signing our latest contract we have witnessed an increase in outsourcing work to countries with a vulnerable workforce that is taken advantage of,” he told Labor Notes . “Giving up the expiration date reduces our time line in securing language to protect our jobs.” Pay for Stability The union’s Region 4 director, Brandon Campbell, who covers the Deere locals, said the company’s proposal could have held advantages for members. “The market is in a downturn, and that will continue into next year,” he said, “especially with the uncertainty of the current presidential administration. Companies love stability; they’ll pay a few extra bucks to have stability, and they can certainly afford a few extra bucks. “I don’t know if 2027 is going to be a great time to be at the table with them. Trump is going to be in office still. That’s not good for UAW working people, after our president [Shawn Fain] wore proudly a ‘Trump is a scab’ shirt. And I did the same. It’s not necessarily a good time to get into that fight with that company.” A two-year extension would push expiration to fall 2029. Former Deere worker Sara Yenzer dug into company finances and wrote on Facebook: What pisses me off about it. Deere says they need this extension for “certainty” and “stability” because of economic volatility. Fine. Except in June, the same month this whole thing kicked off, Deere raised their full-year guidance [what they tell Wall Street about how they expect to do this year] and announced a new stock buyback program [link added]. Analysts read that as Deere signaling they’re confident enough in their cash generation to commit more capital to shareholders. That doesn’t sound like a company *bracing for volatility* to me. Since our 2021 contract, they’ve paid out over $25 billion in shareholder distributions, and they just told Wall Street they’re ready to hand out more. The “volatility” argument only gets applied to us (labor costs) never to what goes out the door to shareholders. Now, with a downturn here they’re asking workers to be flexible. That’s the part that’s bullshit. Lucas DeSpain, assistant director of Region 4 and now running (with Fain, Campbell, and Dickerson) for director on the United UAW slate, replied approvingly, “Sara Yenzer is a hammer and this math is nails.” Deere forecast a fiscal 2026 net income of $4.5 to $5 billion. The slate is asking members to continue the union’s aggressive direction as exemplified by the “stand-up strike ”, other contract campaigns and strikes , and new organizing . Whose Downturn? Dickerson questioned Deere’s finances and its concern for workers, writing, “We see the same industry conditions Deere sees. We also see Deere’s corporate ledger. We see shareholders enjoying the ‘continuity’ of collecting the rewards of our members’ hard work. The people who build the products have earned just as much of a voice in deciding what comes next as the people collecting the dividends.” Responding to the company’s argument about a current market downturn, Tim Cummings told Labor Notes , “The ag market is so unpredictable. Global markets, commodity prices, right now we’re in the middle of global uncertainty that has affected a lot of things. We might have a good year this year, a bad year next year, or multiple-year cycles, a decade of good, five years of bad.” Jake Lane, recently elected to the union’s Agricultural Implement Council, points out that Deere is projected to make close to $17 million in profits in 2024–26. He thinks members should vote no, build a contract campaign for fall 2027, and brew momentum for May Day 2028. As of now, the union is planning a membership vote on August 23, presumably on Deere’s original offer, three days after Deere plans to announce its third-quarter financial results.

articles.title: Dockworkers in Six Countries Announce Day of Strikes and Protests Against War and Genocide
articles.content: Dockworkers unions in France, Greece, Basque Country, Turkey, Morocco, and Italy are calling an international day of action ​ “ against war and militarization” on October 30 . They are demanding an end to ​ “ the genocide of the Palestinian people” and the ​ “ US-Israeli wars of aggression in the Middle East and against Iran.” “ Each union will decide the most appropriate form of mobilization according to its national circumstances, starting from strike action and from a shared commitment to prevent the loading of death and destruction,” reads a joint statement from the unions, which was sent to Workday Magazine and In These Times on July 31 . Together, the unions represent workers at 40 ports in Europe and the Mediterranean, according to the statement. Their call for an escalation emerged from a meeting of the port workers unions held in Istanbul in May. The announcement also expresses ​ “ full solidarity with the peoples of Cuba, Venezuela and Sudan,” and declares that ​ “ ports must not be used for the transport of arms, ammunition, military equipment or troops destined for war zones.” “ No to the war economy, government rearmament plans, and the project of militarization of ports and strategic infrastructure from [the] EU,” the unions assert in their statement. ​ “ Public resources must be used to meet people’s social needs, not to finance war.” Signatories include CGT FNPD in France, ENEDEP in Greece, LAB in Basque Country, LIMAN-IS in Turkey, ODT in Morocco, and ORSA Porti and USB in Italy. A rally of mostly dockworkers in Genoa, Italy, in response to attacks on the Global Sumud Flotilla, on October 3, 2025. Photo by Emanuela Zampa/Getty Images Since October 2023 , Palestinian trade unionists have repeatedly called on union members around the world to go on strike and refuse to handle arms shipments to Israel, to protest the latter’s military campaign in Gaza, which has been denounced as a genocide by leading human rights groups and scholars . (The United States has provided crucial political and financial support to Israel.) On April 5 , 2025 , the General Federation of Trade Unions in Gaza appealed to unionists to ​“create real pressure to stop this dirty war.” Dockworkers have played a spirited role in answering this call. From Belgium to Sweden to Italy, dockworkers have refused to handle weapons components bound for Gaza, and on February 6 , they shut down 21 ports across the Mediterranean, including Bilbao and Tangier, to protest the use of civilian port infrastructure for military purposes, and the incorporation of their jobs into a war economy. The statement follows Italy’s two general strikes in the fall of 2025 in solidarity with Palestinians. Ten months ago, about 60 dockworkers gathered at the Port Authority building in Civitavecchia, a small Italian coastal town northwest of Rome. It was September 22 , 2025 , and they had walked off their jobs earlier that day, shutting down the port as part of a general strike to protest the Italian government’s status as the third largest supplier of arms to Israel. Where they stood, they were surrounded by about 600 people cheering them on — students, teachers, railway workers, public sector workers — a significant crowd for a tiny town. “ It was a beautiful sight to see the dock workers surrounded by their city,” recalls Riccardo Petrarolo, who serves on the national coordination body for Italy’s ports with USB (Unione Sindacale di Base). The dockworkers started getting WhatsApp messages from colleagues in larger cities, like Livorno and Genoa, reporting that workers had shut down their ports, too. And news of strikes and closures were also rolling in from the media. ​ “ They were saying the exact same thing was happening at the other harbors,” Petrarolo says. When the dockworkers announced each new shutdown over a speaker system, Petrarolo tells me, the crowd let out ​ “ a loud cheer, like at a stadium.” The scene around the Trapezio pier in the Port of Salerno on June 9, 2025, where there was an effort to stop a ship thought to have weapons that would be used in the genocide in Gaza. Photo by Ivan Romano/Getty Images These actions are the product of decades of worker-built relationships with Palestinians, and years of organizing against participation in arms shipments. On August 30 , 2025 , 40 , 000 people rallied in Genoa to send off the Global Sumud Flotilla to deliver food and aid to Gaza. For seafaring people — the workers who labor on the docks, load and unload ships, repair and move equipment, and transport goods to other ports — the flotilla’s struggles to reach Gaza resonated deeply, and attacks against the vessel provoked profound anger. Riccardo Rudino, a dockworker with the city’s Autonomous Port Workers’ Collective (CALP), declared to the crowd that sent the ship off, ​ “ If, even for 20 minutes, we lose contact with our comrades on the flotilla, we will block all of Europe: from Genoa’s docks. Not a single nail will leave. It will be a global strike.” Genoa dockworkers soon called for a general strike on September 22 , to protest Italy’s complicity in the onslaught on Gaza, and USB, which has roughly 100 , 000 members in both the private and public sectors, supported the action. About half a million people walked off the job that day, and 1 million took part in protests across Italian towns and cities. Highways, streets, and subways were shut down, as people across the country took up the call, ​ “ Blocchiamo tutto,” or ​ “ Block everything.” José Nivoi, a dockworker and spokesperson for Collettivo Autonomo Lavoratori Portuali (CALP), an independent dockworker union in Genoa, sailed with the Global Sumud Flotilla, and gave an interview from aboard the vessel on September 23 in support of the strike. ​ “ The mobilizations we have been carrying out until recently were totally in support of Palestine and we never backed down,” he said. Then, on October 1 and 2 of 2025 , Israel intercepted the vessels of the flotilla and arrested the hundreds of people on board. The time had come to make good on the threat of ​ “ not a single nail.” Italian organizers responded with an even bigger general strike on October 3 . This time, the Confederazione Generale Italiana del Lavoro (CGIL), the largest union federation in Italy, called for the strike, as did USB. An estimated 2 million people protested in more than 80 cities. Ports and highways were blocked and shut down, rail lines were disrupted, and schools and universities closed. Are you a member of DSA? If so, we've got a free subscription for you to our print magazine. No-strings attached, no credit card necessary, just free for 1 year (that's 10 issues). Scan the QR code in the image or go to www.inthesetimes.com/dsa “ This was organized very quickly and outside of the legal framework in Italy, and as before, involved large and small cities, and many people taking to the streets in solidarity,” says Petrarolo from USB. ​ “ This, of course, involved a reaction from the Italian state, which involved fines to the unions, and police and judicial actions against organizers. But this did not stop the organizing, and the actual result was that the next day 1 million people took to the streets in Rome.” Dockworkers are hoping to build on the momentum. The announcement of the October 30 day of action is based on the ​ “ Istanbul Declaration,” which was endorsed by all signatories. Alongside their anti-war demands, workers are insisting that ​ “ collective agreements must guarantee real wage increases, secure employment, reduced working hours, and fair pension provisions.” And they don’t want mechanization or artificial intelligence to ​ “ eliminate jobs or undermine workers’ rights.” The unions say, ​ “ We are ready to meet with organized groups of dockworkers and port workers from any other ports interested in becoming part of this common struggle.” This article is a joint publication of In These Times and Workday Magazine , a nonprofit newsroom devoted to holding the powerful accountable through the perspective of workers.

articles.title: Russia’s Authoritarian Neoliberalism Reaches Its Limits
articles.author: Jeremy Morris
articles.content: While Russian forces nightly attack Ukrainian cities with long-range missiles — killing increasing numbers of civilians since the reduction of US military aid to Kyiv — this year has seen Ukraine escalate its own long-range campaign against Russia. Drones have targeted two types of infrastructure important to Russians’ sense of normality: the logistics hubs for Wildberries , an Amazon-style online marketplace which is Russia’s single largest goods distribution network , and, perhaps more importantly, petrol and diesel fuel refineries, which appear to be relatively easy targets and a weak link in the overall domestic economy. Beyond the battlefield, responses within Russian society matter to the Kremlin’s chances of keeping the war effort going. It appears increasingly likely that after another set of falsified parliamentary elections this September, it will attempt a renewed form of compulsory military mobilization . Such a policy was briefly tried in late 2022 but soon proved a political failure and was abandoned in favor of mercenary payments. This latter approach now appears to be reaching its limits, however, after exhausting the reserve populations of potential recruits among both ethnic minorities and Russians in disadvantaged regions. There is already increasing fatigue and discontent with the war’s enormous human cost and parlous effect on the economy. If severe demographic decline wasn’t bad enough, then revisiting the politically taboo topic of military conscription will bring, if not open political crisis, at least a more febrile atmosphere of fear and yearning for change. What we don’t know yet is what the texture of this political moment will feel like. It may be “hot” and prickly like the painful mass mobilizations around the late 1980s–early ’90s, or else it may feel, as it sometimes did for the rearguard civil society that bravely resisted the slide into autocracy in the late 2000s, like wading through sand while being pursued by an implacable horde. In this lies a deeper point about how we understand Russia. As we approach this conjuncture of social, geopolitical, and economic forces, much of what we don’t know is because of the narrowness and superficiality of how we often make sense of Russian society. Blind Spots One of the main blind spots in expert commentary stems from groupthink about the nature of Russian society: it is essentialized as passive, atomized, and largely supine. Rarely do the legions of armchair observers move beyond such caricature, because they are reliant on an ecosystem of opinion consensus by measurement, which is itself partly incorporated into Putinism’s media management. Pollsters present Russians with the correct framing: “The conduct of the armed forces in Ukraine — do you support it?” And dutifully a majority in favor is produced. Even on its own terms, though, cracks begin to show, such as a recent poll that found only 30 percent favor continuing the war — even within what is obviously a self-selected sample of mainly loyalist citizens willing to invite a pollster into their home. Opinion polls and interpretation of elite discussion: that’s the extent of the current Kremlinology. There is a strong allergy to field data and field experts, partly as a result of the retreat of area expertise in the United States. As a result, the Washington-centric common sense about Russia is hegemonic. In June–July, two worthy think tanks, Carnegie and Kennan , both published questionable versions of an argument about a renewed rally-’round-the-flag effect in response to the step change in Ukrainian attacks. To me, as one of the last of a breed of anthropologists examining politics from below, there is a disturbing groupthink around the idea that Russians are enthusiastic for the war and its aims, even as it becomes impossible to ignore the costs within Russia. Speaking to any selection of ordinary people, it’s clear that a large majority want the war to end now, on any terms short of having to pay reparations. But arguments about public sentiment merely reinforce the sense that we are not even able to articulate a language that would facilitate a discussion about the longer-term crisis in Russia, of which the war is just a symptom. The invasion of Ukraine is not a departure from the normality of Putinism, but rather the morbid culmination of a socioeconomic crisis inherent to authoritarian neoliberal governance. For over two decades, the regime operated as a distillation of unbridled political power bent on accumulation of economic rents, insider ownership, and constellations of patron-client control. It did this while starving the social state: a system characterized by astute observers like Nick Trickett as an “empire of austerity.” One reason for the catastrophic outcome of the security elite’s decision to go to war is that this same elite failed to understand how weak Russian society had become because of a systematic refusal to invest in public goods beyond the bare minimum required to mitigate immediate crisis. This war is the gangrenous result of a system that has long prioritized the protection of a tiny rapacious elite over the basic survival of its population. As I argue in my recent book on the war and its less proximate causes, Russia has become a state-of-the-art laboratory for the production of poverty and the imposition of neoliberal rationality — one that is now admired especially by a similar breed of political capitalists in the orbit of Donald Trump and beyond it. Unlike the caricatures in Western media, the Russian state is not a throwback to Soviet planning. Rather, it drives market-oriented subjectivities where the individual is forced to become a contestant in a nightmarish game of social reproduction, in an atmosphere of cynicism and disregard for human costs. This system has successfully depoliticized social inequality, framing the divide between winners and losers as a matter of personal failure rather than structural dispossession. Putinism’s legitimacy has rested on a hollowed-out social compact: the state provides the veneer of a convenient consumer culture, symbolized by the platform-capitalism world of ubiquitous brands like Wildberries, in exchange for political passivity. Yet this convenience masks a brutal socioeconomic Darwinism where representatives of the elite and government, including those who oversaw the deindustrialization of the country, the legalized theft of its remaining assets, and the casting into poverty of tens of millions in the 1990s, like to hold forth about Russians’ inherent bovine mentality. They are called mindless munchers of coarse feed, inured to suffering and privation, who expect handouts and a paternal state while not understanding that “man is wolf to man,” as the saying goes, and that the government “owes you nothing.” Since the 2008 financial crisis, Russians have faced some of the worst developed-world income stagnation and a wealth concentration that is significantly higher than in the United States or China. Putinism has responded to this long-term decay not with reinvestment of its petrochemical bounty, but with a neoconservative “cultural war” against Western “permissiveness,” using “sovereign democracy” as a shield to protect the ill-gotten gains of a security-state elite. Observers often rely on a poorly fitting translation from a very different cultural and historical context — the United States after 9/11 and a rally-’round-the-flag narrative — to explain what seems to be Russians’ lack of resistance to the war, or even enthusiasm for it. By contrast, I prefer to think in terms of a defensive consolidation. Russians have not “rallied” to patriotic fervor; rather, they have retreated into comforting narratives of encirclement and civilizational peril, some of which align with propaganda but others which do not. They do this to manage both long-term socioeconomic trauma and a sense of helplessness exacerbated by the war and its resulting stresses. After the invasion in 2022, many consolidated behind the Putinite authorities out of a desperate unspoken hope: that the war would finally break the dismal neoliberal compact and force the state to return to a more prosocial collectivist project reminiscent of the Soviet era’s social guarantees. Military Keynesianism? However, this hope for a more protective state has proven illusory. The “military Keynesianism” touted by both the Kremlin and certain segments of the Left who claim that the working classes are “winning” from the war economy is a fantasy. While there was short-lived growth in real incomes, peaking in 2024, this “multiplier effect” was geographically delimited and has already been devoured by inflation, the resulting massive hike in bank rates, and the hard capacity limits of an economy plagued by a lack of investment. The “social elevator” of war money is reaching its limit, and the structural power of labor remains suppressed by a legal environment that makes defending workers’ rights nearly impossible. The true unraveling of the Putin era will not be found in the dream come true of a revolutionary democratizing subject, which is what Alexei Navalny embodied until his murder by the state. The emotional investment by the West, by the Russian liberals, and by the pundit class in figures like Navalny has led to an analytical myopia. Rather than the smart and charismatic leader featured in Forbes fifteen times between his arrest in 2021 and death in 2024, a much more likely figure to exploit a future crisis, or even precipitate, it will be a composite character embodying features more reminiscent of the 1990s: a red-brown politician from within the existing security elite, promising to resolve the contradiction between spectacular elite wealth and everyday insecurity. This is because the reality of rising inequality meeting austerity and the inability of a state to ensure basic human needs like adequate health care remains more “real” to Russians than the war itself. Despite the “military Keynesian” rhetoric, measurable inequality remains as stark as ever, with the top 1 percent holding 70 percent of all assets. Russia is an outlier among countries rated as high on the human development index, with 10 percent of the population receiving half of all income, and 96 percent of savers have negligible savings. The tax system is a masterpiece of regressive redistribution. The state funds its war through sales taxes and fees as much as by selling oil and gas. These taxes fall disproportionately on the poor, while a much-lauded flat income tax ensures that even those in extreme poverty pay a higher relative burden than those with assets. There is no wealth tax, and inheritance tax was abolished nearly twenty years ago to help protect the transition of wealth within the plutocracy. This is the context in which we must view the recent attacks on Wildberries infrastructure. These attacks strike at the heart of the convenient consumer culture that substituted for political legitimacy among the urban middle class. When these logistics hubs are targeted, it strips away the last remaining mask of the neoliberal compact. Putinism cannot provide security, it cannot provide social mobility, and now it can no longer guarantee the frictionless consumption economy that was built on the backs of an exploited, micro-proletarianized workforce. Conditions of Protest Periods of apparently immovable political order have often seen growing reservoirs of popular grievance that unexpectedly emerge when existing ways of accommodating to the system fail. Catherine II confronted enormous peasant rebellion despite presiding over one of the strongest imperial states in Europe. The revolutions of 1905 and 1917 emerged from societies long considered politically pacified. The Novocherkassk massacre of 1962 reminded Soviet authorities that workers remained capable of seemingly spontaneous collective resistance despite extensive brutalization. The coal miners’ strikes of 1989 helped destabilize a system that had appeared institutionally impregnable only a few years earlier. More recently, the labor disputes, social protests against loss of benefits and pensions, environmental campaigns, and local civic mobilizations against housing demolitions of the 2000s and 2010s demonstrated that collective action never disappeared beneath Putinism; it simply operated in fragmented and localized forms typical of what might be called a refined and relatively polite form of classic authoritarianism. Before the war, labor-related protests were at a record high despite legal repression of unions and, essentially, a ban on legal industrial actions. Labor actions alone are unlikely to develop into political protests. Yet they might, as the leading researcher Pyotr Bizyukov argues, create conditions for other forms of political resistance to emerge. Today micropolitical resistance is already fermenting, from the sabotage of military draft offices to online activists showing people how to avoid mobilization. Indeed, it is hard to keep track of the many groups still organizing, albeit clandestinely or online and abroad. As I argue in my book, the memory of a future-orientated “commonality” (in Russian: obshchnost ) and the ideal of an achievable, if flawed, postcapitalist society that provided public goods to all remain alive, represents a lasting political stumbling block to the regime’s largely empty rhetoric and inability to offer Russians better prospects. Even Vladimir Putin seemed to confront this fact recently when asked an “astonishing” question about what positive roles Russians will be able to look forward to after the war. He clearly found it surprising, when confronted by an ordinary person with the age-old Russian question: “what is to be done”? He interpreted this as about people’s need to be incorporated into a “great cause.” As the country enters a period of stagflation and illusions in the war economy dissolve, the refusal of the state to recognize that its main purpose is to ensure the social reproduction of its people may finally meet the historical limit of Russians’ patience. In its great laboratory of dispossession, exploitation, and now battlefield disposal, the vanguard of authoritarian neoliberalism has long treated ordinary Russians as biopolitical waste. Now, four years into a war even Russia’s leaders can no longer explain, this elite is entering into sharper confrontation with this same people.
