articles.title: Community College Faculty and Staff, Suffering Low Pay and Board Hostility, Fight for a Contract
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: By: Jason M, Jake S WORCESTER – Teachers and staff organized under the Massachusetts Community College Council (MCCC) have been engaged in contract negotiations with the Massachusetts Board of Higher Education for the last few months. Despite Massachusetts offering free community college through the MassEducate program, faculty at community colleges across the state face conditions that harm their wellbeing. Low pay, food insecurity, and ever-increasing class sizes hurt faculty and prevent them from being able to teach their students. While community college presidents across the state regularly make more than $200,000 annually, community college faculty make the lowest average salary nationwide, according to a study conducted by the Massachusetts Teachers Association (MTA). Nearly half of MCCC members struggle with food insecurity and most need a second job to pay their bills. Increases in the size of online classes by as much as 56% undermines existing protections in the Local QCC Distance Education agreement and severely hampers the ability of faculty and staff to offer students a quality education. The Massachusetts Board of Higher Education has not entertained a proposal from MCCC. Only three bargaining sessions have been held over a four-month period, during which the Board has tried to implement restrictions over rank-and-file MCCC members’ ability to attend, and changes to how union representatives are compensated for their time spent negotiating. The union has filed an Unfair Labor Practice (ULP) over the latter. Working Mass sat down with Caitlin B, an academic advisor and enrollment counselor, as well as secretary for the union’s QCC chapter (the Quinsigamond Community College Professional Association, or QCCPA), to talk about union members’ concerns. Quotations used in this article have been edited for clarity and brevity. Distraction, Delay, and Hostility Salary, workload, and schedule flexibility are top concerns amongst QCCPA members. The Mass Board of Higher Ed, instead of entertaining proposals from the union, has forced negotiations to fixate around rules of engagement. Caitlin explained: We haven’t proposed anything regarding these issues yet. So far, we’ve been working with management on establishing ground rules for bargaining. This has already been difficult to negotiate. The Mass Board of Higher Education has also earned an Unfair Labor Practice charge from QCCPA early on by undermining compensation of the union’s bargaining team. They don’t want us to be compensated, so we’ve been doing all of our bargaining outside of working hours. I’ve never done this before, but other people are like: ‘This is absurd.’ The school argues that rank-and-file union members should not be physically visible to the boss when they attend virtual bargaining sessions. I’ve heard horror stories about bargaining, and so far I haven’t experienced anything that bad, but this year, there were some issues with silent representatives. Dues-paying members can silently attend bargaining sessions, and there’s this complaint about, should they be visible during the Zoom session, should they not be visible, it clogs things up, blah blah blah. The Board of Higher Education hasn’t offered much detail to explain why seeing union members’ faces make them so uncomfortable during negotiations. Caitlin can only assume their intent. The silent representatives are really important for us, because when we caucus in between bargaining sessions, they actually have information they can give to us that we wouldn’t necessarily know off the cuff. Management doesn’t want them there, they don’t want to look at people when they’re telling them: ‘No, you can’t get this, you can’t get that’, so that’s been the biggest issue for them right now.” A Real Sense of Ownership When asked about what being in a union meant to her, Caitlin paused thoughtfully. Without the union, we’d be at the mercy of whatever our employee decides what is best for us. When you work in a system with so many different components and types of employees, having proper representation is essential. Caitlin continued: My coworkers have an unwavering dedication to their students. We work together on a mission to help our students get what they need, and at the community college level, our students may not be “traditional.” We are their advocates and support systems, and that is something worth preserving. Caitlin reflected positively on rank-and-file engagement at QCC. We’ve increased our membership a bit. We’ve got the MTA [Massachusetts Teachers Association, of which MCCC is an affiliate] noticing that and coming to our meetings every week, they’re really paying attention to how we’re doing things, which is really nice. So I think watching the change, watching people being more engaged in it, makes you want to be more engaged in it. Caitlin in large part credited James L, president of the QCC chapter of MCCC and an active member of Worcester DSA who previously served on its Steering Committee, with this growth. “He quickly formed an organizing committee on campus, which exists at the statewide level, but usually locals don’t have one,” she explained. I think once people started realizing, oh, we can actually do something with this, it’s not just a contract, it’s also action, you know? I think that’s really important. Workers united can, in fact, demand a say in the place where their labor is bought and sold is why a strong, conscious labor movement is a central component to building working class power. Ownership unites the collective. When workers organize amongst themselves to confront a class enemy, they become the protagonists of the struggle they live through every day. They learn to think and act collectively, laying down the paving stones along the road to a better future. One where the working class is in full control of society, not the bosses and the capitalists. Jason M and Jake S are members of Central Mass and Worcester DSA. They are contributing authors for Working Mas s. . The post Community College Faculty and Staff, Suffering Low Pay and Board Hostility, Fight for a Contract appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: DSA Statement on the New State Department Report on Cuba
articles.author: DSA National Statements
articles.content: DSA stands unwaveringly against Donald Trump, Marco Rubio, and the billionaire class’ attempts to repress and silence our movement to end the United States’ genocidal blockade against Cuba. From NSPM-7 to Marco Rubio’s “Cuba Report” released by the State Department, we know that they lack any legal basis to respond to the democratic power of the working class. They cannot fathom the idea that the multi-racial, international working class can join forces and organize together organically, free from the influence of any foreign government. We are being depicted as fanatics for building a world where people live in peace, safe from bombs; where no child goes hungry; where no family has to worry that their lives will be ripped apart by ICE; and where no one has to suffer from lack of housing or healthcare. They depict us as such because they are afraid that our ideas are not fringe demands. These are the demands that millions of Americans have already committed to fighting for at the ballot box and in the streets. Despite Rubio’s attempt to smear us, his report admits that DSA does not organize on behalf of the Cuban Government, only of its own accord. In DSA, organizing of our own accord means fulfilling the democratically-made decisions of our members. Our internationalism is rooted in the principles of our members who channel their support for socialism around the world into campaigns that confront imperialism and transcend the walls it constructs between the workers of the world. Through this difficult period, our Cuba Solidarity organizing has remained successful and we are committed to continuing our organizing against the blockade of Cuba by the United States and to assist the Cuban people against the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe that has ensued. As Black and brown socialists gain political power and mainstream visibility, it’s not lost on us that the Trump administration is attempting to paint anti-racist organizing as a coordinated plot against the United States, rather than an organic expression of resistance to centuries of oppression. This is not new. We know from history that our Black, Native, and immigrant neighbors are the first to be targeted. We reject the report’s characterization of the movements for Democracy and Black Liberation as foreign influenced and condemn these claims as racist and absurd. Our comrades have expressed their constitutionally-protected rights to express, organize, and assemble and we stand in unwavering solidarity with them as they continue to do so. Movements for Democracy, Socialism, and Black Liberation are always intentionally smeared as dangerous because they are threats to the status quo — a status quo where trillionaires exist while the masses struggle to afford groceries, where workers struggle to breathe as they are forced to toil through increasingly dangerous heatwaves and toxic wildfire smoke. This report is an attempt to scapegoat Cuba as some puppet-master behind the strife here in the United States, it is a tool for fulfilling Rubio and Trump’s personal goals of regime change, no matter the human cost. As Trump’s minions weaponize state resources against our movements, they show that there is no law, domestic or international, strong enough alone to protect our freedom of speech and assembly. The only way to defeat this tyrannical regime is by building a mass movement in solidarity with all working people around the world suffering under the boot of US imperialism; a movement powerful enough to demand a new world, one our children deserve to inherit. !Cuba Si, Bloqueo No! articles.title: Coordination is Complicity: Reject Operation Stonegarden
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: ROC DSA Steering Committee – August 10, 2026 On August 11, 2026, the Monroe County Legislature will vote whether to accept $161,285 for Operation Stonegarden, a grant funding local law enforcement participation in a federal border security program tied to Customs and Border Protection (CBP). Legislators must vote NO. Coordination with the agencies carrying out Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda is complicity. Operation Stonegarden would increase cooperation and intelligence sharing between local law enforcement and immigration agents, and fund surveillance technology like license plate readers. These are the same agents who are infiltrating our community and deporting our neighbors. We cannot empower them through increased material support and data. Supporters of this legislation say it’s the same money the County has approved for years. Setting aside whether it was ever appropriate to accept this grant, it is undeniable that this time is different. Removal orders neared 500,000 in 2025, up by more than 56% from the year prior, and more than 65,000 people are currently in ICE detention, the majority of whom have no criminal record. The racial content of Trump’s policies is clear, and the County must refuse to be connected with those responsible for their enactment. We are disappointed by Democrats who voted this legislation out of committee on July 28. They have had the opportunity to reflect, and we hope they have found the moral courage to vote NO on August 11. We applaud those who have demonstrated commitment to human rights by consistently opposing this legislation. Opposition to Operation Stonegarden is just the start. ROC DSA calls on our representatives to support policies that ensure all County residents are safe from these anti-immigrant attacks. The County must formally bar cooperation with immigration enforcement, and use our economic leverage to divest from companies supporting Trump’s agenda. Which way, resistance or complicity? articles.title: Francesca Hong on What Democratic Socialism Means to Her
articles.content: On August 11 , Wisconsin voters will decide the next Democratic nominee for governor, and State Assembly Member Francesca Hong is leading in the polls. Hong is running with the backing of local chapters of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), along with a number of labor unions, grassroots organizations, progressive groups and state elected officials. Hong is the first Asian American elected to the State Assembly and is running in a state that President Donald Trump won twice, but that also boasts a proud socialist history going back more than a century. Wisconsin is the state that produced the idea of ​ “ sewer socialism” which Mayor Zohran Mamdani is now harkening back to under his administration in New York City. As the first open socialist in the Washington State Legislature since 1914 , I wanted to learn more from Hong about how she views the the power of state government to secure meaningful material wins for working people. I spoke with her in early August, when she explained to me, ​ “ I want working people to have a meaningful voice not only at the ballot box, but in their workplaces, their communities and the economy.” This interview has been edited for clarity and length. As a democratic socialist, what problems did you seek to solve by running for public office, and why did you believe that the Wisconsin State Assembly would be the place to solve them? I had spent my career in the service industry. I was a dishwasher, a line cook, a chef, a small business owner and a single mom. When Covid- 19 hit, I watched an entire industry shut down almost overnight. Workers who had spent years creating enormous value suddenly had no paycheck, no healthcare and no support from the government that should be taking care of its people. Small businesses were fighting to survive while the largest corporations had access to resources the rest of us could only dream of. People like me were left blaming themselves and feeling like failures, but it’s the system that was failing us. The situation we were in was the result of political choices. I ran for office to be part of the solution. The Assembly was a great starting point because so many of these choices happen at the state level. States determine wages and worker protections. We fund public schools. We administer Medicaid. We decide how much power local governments have to raise revenue, build housing or invest in transit. We regulate utilities and corporations. We write the rules that determine whether working people have power in the workplace and whether families can afford the basic necessities of life. I ran because I understood that government is one arena where working people have to build power, and because decisions were being made there every day that shaped whether my neighbors could live with dignity. I know from personal experience that being a socialist in an American legislative body can be a lonely and difficult experience. What were some of the fights you took on as an assemblymember? For the entirety of my time in office, I’ve served in a legislature controlled by Republicans, so I learned very quickly that you have to define success more broadly than whether leadership allows your bill to receive a vote. I’ve introduced an Economic Justice Bill of Rights because I believe healthcare, housing, education, food and a dignified job should be understood as basic economic rights. I’ve fought to raise the minimum wage and advocated for paid family and medical leave. I’ve introduced legislation to provide healthy school meals for every child and restore the collective bargaining rights that were stripped from Wisconsin workers under Act 10 . Sometimes, the objective is shifting the conversation around an idea that people initially tell you is impossible. Sometimes it’s using the legislature to give organizers, workers and communities a platform. And sometimes you find openings to actually change the law. I was proud to help pass bipartisan legislation requiring Wisconsin schools to teach Asian American and Hmong American history, a victory that grew out of community organizing and building positive relationships with folks from across the aisle. That experience has reinforced something I believe deeply: elected officials should not think of themselves as the movement. Our job is to open doors, bring organizing into the institution, use the power we have to shift material conditions and make it easier for people outside the Capitol to build power. A socialist legislator without an organized constituency can be isolated. A socialist legislator connected to workers, unions and community organizations can make the institution much less comfortable with the status quo. What would you say are some barriers to the achievement of democratic socialist policies in elected government? The biggest barrier is institutional power. People sometimes talk about progressive policy as though the obstacle is simply finding the right data to back up your policy or persuading enough legislators that an idea makes sense. But many of the systems we’re trying to change are working exactly as intended for the people who benefit from them. Corporations have lobbyists in the Capitol every day. Wealthy interests provide financial backing for campaigns and organizations designed to shape the policy conversation. Legislative leaders can keep overwhelmingly popular proposals from ever receiving a hearing or vote. And in Wisconsin, years of gerrymandering allowed Republicans to maintain enormous legislative power even in a closely divided state. There is also a political culture that treats scarcity as inevitable. We are constantly told that universal programs are unrealistic while enormous subsidies, tax breaks and giveaways to corporations are treated as the natural order of things. That is why electoral politics can’t be separated from organizing. Winning a seat is not the end of the work. If you want to change who has power, you have to build durable organizations outside of government that can make demands of those inside it. I think that’s particularly important for socialists serving in state legislatures. We should pass legislation wherever we can, but we should also use these offices to expose who benefits from the current system, raise expectations about what government can provide, and help build the working-class coalition capable of making change unavoidable. You made the decision to join DSA during a difficult time in state and local politics, 2020 . What moved you to join the organization, and how long have you identified as a democratic socialist? I joined DSA in 2020 because the organization was fighting for the things that had already come to define my politics: raising wages, racial justice, worker power and an economy that serves working people instead of an increasingly concentrated group of wealthy and corporate interests. My politics grew out of lived experience and community organizing more than a particular label. I spent my adult life working alongside people who could work incredibly hard and still be one emergency away from losing everything. I watched service workers create thriving businesses and communities without receiving the stability, healthcare or wages they deserved in return. I saw how race, class and gender shaped who had power and who was expected to bear the burden when things went wrong. To me, democratic socialism is about democracy, fairness and human rights. Working people should have a real say in the decisions that shape their lives, not just in government, but in their workplaces and in the economy. Too often, the most essential parts of our lives, from what we’re paid to what we spend on healthcare, housing and utilities, are determined by corporations with far more power than the people they serve. I want working people to have a meaningful voice not only at the ballot box, but in their workplaces, their communities and the economy. And I believe that government should guarantee the basic conditions people need to actually exercise that freedom: healthcare, housing, education, childcare, a living wage and the right to organize. As a 501 © 3 nonprofit organization, In These Times does not support or oppose any candidate for elected office.

articles.title: How Argentina Banned Its Opposition
articles.author: Delfina Rossi
articles.content: Imagine the person you had already decided to vote for in the next election — the leader your side trusts most, the one whose name you would put on a ballot without a second thought. Not a fringe figure. Not someone caught enriching himself or credibly accused of ordering a killing on a street corner. Imagine waking to the news that they will not be on that ballot at all, because a court has decided that the ordinary business of governing — a contract signed, a subsidy approved, a program launched, a budget enacted — was in fact a crime and has sent them to prison for it and barred them from public life for good. Hold that person in your mind, whoever they are. For half the country it is a Democrat; for the other half a Republican. That is precisely the point. Every leader who has actually governed leaves behind a record of contestable decisions — the substance of governing is nothing but contestable decisions — and any of them can later be reread by a motivated prosecutor and an obliging court, not as policy but as felony. The machinery does not care who you voted for. It needs only a target and a tribunal. Most citizens, whatever their politics, would know at once what they were looking at. Not the rule of law but its inversion: the courts turned into the instrument for removing the opponent the ballot box would not. They would understand that a republic in which the state can jail and disqualify the front-runner by criminalizing the acts of government has stopped being a democracy in any sense that matters — and that the elections held afterward, however clean the count, are hollow at the core. For Argentines, none of this requires imagination. It is simply the news. Banished From Office for Life That politician is Cristina Fernández de Kirchner. Twice elected president and later elected vice president, she has never lost a national election. Today she is the head of the Partido Justicialista and remains the most formidable figure Argentine politics has produced this century. Her political stature has been likened to Eva Perón’s. Since June 2025, however, Kirchner has been a prisoner. Because she is over seventy, she serves her sentence under house arrest in an apartment on 1111 San José street in Buenos Aires. An electronic ankle bracelet tracks her movements. Her visitors are restricted by court order. Even her access to her own rooftop has become a matter for federal litigation. This month, an appeals court again refused to loosen those conditions. Her sentence — six years in prison and permanent disqualification from public office — is final. She will not appear on the ballot in 2027. She will not appear on any ballot again. The case that produced this, known as Vialidad , concerned the administration of public roadworks contracts in the southern province of Santa Cruz. It is worth being specific about what the conviction rests on, because the details comprise the argument. The expert report propping up the fraud allegation examined only five of fifty-one road projects. The tribunal itself conceded it had no direct proof of criminal conduct and had built its case on inference. The Supreme Court that made the conviction has been whittled down to three judges. Even Raúl Zaffaroni, a former Supreme Court justice and hardly a fringe voice, has observed that no serious country entrusts its highest court to a panel of three. Several of the judges who handled the case at various stages maintain well-documented social ties with Mauricio Macri, the conservative president under whom the prosecution took shape. Kirchner was the perfect enemy for Macri and the Argentinian right: a woman, a Peronist, and a champion of wealth distribution. From Tanks to Courts It is worth remembering too that the courtroom was not the first venue tried. In September 2022, as the prosecution reached its climax, a man pushed through the crowd outside Kirchner’s home, raised a pistol to her face, and pulled the trigger twice. The gun did not fire. Years on, the question of who, if anyone, directed him remains unanswered. One of the country’s largest newspapers captured the sequence in a much-discussed headline of the period: the bullet that did not go off, and the judgment that would . The bullet failed. The judgment did not. Argentines have a word for what is being done to Kirchner, and it is not one they coined for the occasion: “proscripción” — proscription. After the 1955 coup that overthrew Juan Domingo Perón, Peronism — the movement of the country’s organized working class, and for most of that period its electoral majority — was banned outright from national elections for eighteen years. Its leader lived in exile; its candidates were struck from ballots; its very name was, for a time, illegal to print. The generals and their civilian allies understood something their descendants understand still: when a movement rooted among workers and the poor keeps winning, the simplest way to govern against the majority is to prevent the majority from choosing. What has changed since 1955 is only the instrument. Where they once relied on tanks and decrees, they now use indictments and three-judge courts. Argentine Lawfare This is what the shorthand “lawfare” names — not a conspiracy theory but a recognizable, recurrent pattern with its own grammar, one that has run through the region this century. Fernando Lugo removed in Paraguay by a two-day impeachment. Dilma Rousseff removed in Brazil over budgetary accounting. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva jailed and barred from office before ultimately being vindicated. Rafael Correa convicted in Ecuador and driven into exile. Evo Morales disqualified in Bolivia. The details differ; the choreography does not: a compliant judiciary, a concentrated media that reaches its verdict before the courts do, a foreign policy establishment that blesses the result, and always — always — a target who governed for the wrong people. Argentines will go to the polls in 2027 in a country where the leader of the largest opposition party sits under guard in her apartment, barred from the ballot. The votes will almost certainly be counted honestly. That is exactly what makes the situation so instructive and so grim: you can hollow out a democracy without ever touching the count simply by deciding in advance who is allowed to run. So, return to the thought experiment, because it is not really a hypothetical — it is a translation of what is already happening. If you would recognize the jailing and disqualification of the candidate you meant to vote for as a democratic crisis, then you already understand what is happening in Buenos Aires.

articles.title: The Union Deal That’s Undermining Gig Workers
articles.author: Brian Dolber
articles.content: In recent months, unions in the United States and Canada have been claiming victory in gig worker organizing. In May 2026, Uber settled its first collective bargaining agreement with drivers in Victoria, British Columbia. Massachusetts has recognized a union representing seventy thousand Uber drivers, constituting what labor leaders describe as “the largest private-sector organizing win” since the United Auto Workers unionized the Ford Motor Company in 1941. This long-standing record has since been outdone again as the Service Employees International Union (SEIU)–affiliated California Gig Workers Union was named the “union of record” to represent potentially two hundred thousand app-based drivers in the state, establishing “the largest union of gig rideshare drivers in the world.” Legislation allowing drivers collective bargaining rights has also passed in Illinois. All of this, on the surface, enables the possibility for record numbers of workers to be brought into the labor movement. That companies like Uber and Lyft would allow workers to have a say in their own pay and conditions — when their entire business model has been predicated on flouting labor law through misclassification — would be remarkable, and undoubtedly signal that we have reached a turning point within the struggles for gig worker justice and, more broadly, within platform capitalism. If only it were true. For years, worker-to-worker organizing efforts have raised the alarm on platform capitalism’s hyperexploitation. App-based workers demand fair pay, transparency, due process in deactivations, and the protections that come with employee status. Rideshare Drivers United (RDU) in California, for example, emerged out of efforts to challenge low pay and unfair deactivations by drivers who first met each other at the Los Angeles International Airport lot. Using social media and a purpose-built app called Solidarity Tech, drivers scaled up their organizing capacity, ultimately leading a global strike in May 2019 on the eve of Uber’s initial public offering (IPO). The App Drivers and Couriers Union in the United Kingdom organized similarly without the institutional support of Trades Union Council affiliates. In New York, Los Deliveristas Unidos has built solidarity among the largely immigrant delivery workforce along the lines of the worker center model, while the New York Taxi Workers Alliance — an affiliate of the AFL-CIO without any collective bargaining rights — has fought tirelessly and successfully for regulation of the rideshare industry. Scaled up and in alliance with unions that prioritize building bottom-up driver power, self-organized platform worker organizations could significantly improve hundreds of thousands of lives. Such an approach would help ground the struggle against Silicon Valley and AI within immigrant working-class communities. It could be a central strategy in the larger struggle against authoritarianism. But the window of opportunity for labor to facilitate rank-and-file organizing among the most precarious workers in today’s volatile political economy seems to be closing. Legislation extending collective bargaining rights to gig workers has positioned SEIU locals to represent hundreds of thousands of gig workers. Signaling a settlement between labor and industry on the gig work question, this deserves critical attention. From Neutrality Agreements to Partnerships Since the 1990s, unions have sought neutrality agreements with private employers, allowing staff organizers to sign up members and avoid the extreme retaliation workers face in the National Labor Relations Board process. The late labor organizer and strategist Jane McAlevey critiqued this approach for relying on top-down campaigns as “shortcuts” around the deep organizing needed to win strong contracts and sustain a worker-driven movement. The gig economy has magnified this challenge as platforms circumvented labor law through worker misclassification. Uber came to a $100 million class action settlement in Massachusetts and California, agreeing to help form “driver associations.” While the attorney representing the drivers said that these organizations “can play a role similar to a union,” one key difference is that — exempt from the National Labor Relations Act of 1935 (NLRA) and the Fair Labor Standards Act — Uber could play a role in funding these groups. Uber formed the Independent Drivers Guild ( IDG ) in partnership with the International Association of Machinists (IAM) in New York and ultimately also brought this approach to both Massachusetts and Illinois. While drivers organized independently in these states for years, IAM and SEIU have sought to make deals with Uber behind closed doors while advocating for state-level legislative reforms. Forming the Massachusetts App Drivers Union, the Machinists joined forces with SEIU and its building service Local 32BJ and supported extending collective bargaining rights. Together they won the right to bargain with Uber not through the mass organization of seventy thousand drivers across the state but through a ballot measure in 2024. California rideshare drivers won collective bargaining rights through legislation, but drivers had little say in what this legislation would look like. It came through a deal brokered between Gov. Gavin Newsom, Uber and Lyft, and SEIU California. In exchange for the company’s support, SEIU sponsored SB 371 , which reduces the companies’ mandate to provide coverage for accidents — from up to $1 million in damages to $60,000 per person — where the app-based driver is not at fault. The Misclassification Consensus Uber’s willingness to work with major unions has been predicated on conceding that app-based workers would not be classified as employees. While this may be seen as a labor victory, app-based drivers will be negotiating from a far worse position than classified employees do. As misclassified workers, drivers have no effective minimum wage. Laws like California’s Prop 22 mandate that drivers be paid 1.5 times the local minimum wage, but it is only based on “engaged time” — the time from when a driver accepts a ride to when they drop the passenger off at arrival. The time between rides, determined by algorithmic management, is unpaid. AB 1340 names earnings as an optional — not required — topic of sectoral bargaining. Drivers’ low wages are further eaten up by the high expenses on their own vehicles, gas, upkeep, and insurance. As employees, US workers are reimbursed at the Internal Revenue Service rate, currently at ¢72.5 per mile, for driving as part of their job. This all amounts to a significant amount of money that workers must take out of their own paychecks to cover ever increasing gas prices and auto repair costs. A 2022 collaborative study between Rideshare Drivers United and PolicyLink found that the median net income was $6.20 per hour, and the lowest amount any driver in the study earned was $4.10 per hour, after all expenses and all on-app time were considered. Drivers would earn roughly $11 more per hour if they were classified as employees. As independent contractors, drivers will have to negotiate themselves out of this massive deficit just to attain what should be the bare legal minimum. Large unions are trading away these rights in exchange for sectoral agreements that minimize the voices of workers themselves. Sectoral Bargaining or Company Union 2.0? Rather than requiring majority support from a bargaining unit, the legislation and agreements between Uber and large unions all set low thresholds necessary to certify a bargaining agent — 25 percent in Massachusetts and Minnesota, and 30 percent in California. In California, a union will be given the information for all “active drivers” — those who have completed twenty rides in the prior six months — after attaining signatures from 10 percent of the proposed unit. AB 1340 mandates that the unit in California comprise the entire state, an estimated two hundred thousand drivers. With such low thresholds, critics emphasize that workers will not be able “to meaningfully decide, as a group, whether to accept or reject the bargain” to ensure “procedural fairness . . . and that any bargain is substantively good for the workers affected.” Although democratic worker-led organizing could help push for stronger sectoral agreements, this approach to sectoral bargaining seems poised to require little rank-and-file commitment or risk. Legal scholar Veena Dubal notes that unions and platform companies have been discussing sectoral agreements behind closed doors since 2019 to the exclusion of drivers. As such, language in AB 1340 ensures that SEIU Locals 721 and 1021 — the major public employee unions in southern and northern California, respectively with a combined membership of 160,000 workers — are effectively the only unions eligible for recognition. Workers didn’t have much of a choice. IAM has long taken money from Uber to support the work of IDG in New York. Uber has also partnered with existing powerful unions in Australia and the UK to create similar arrangements. The new wave of laws and agreements suggests the expansion of this strategy, allowing for companies to funnel money to unions through deactivation clinic partnerships. Such agreements’ legality are based on gig workers being exempt from the NLRA but being governed under the state-level legislation and enforced by public employee relations boards. Perhaps most devastatingly, the legislation is unclear as to whether drivers have the right to strike as independent contractors. Without the ability to collectively withhold labor, what leverage would they have in negotiations? At best, the proposed model constitutes a shortcut around deep organizing to gain representation of hundreds of thousands of workers. At worst, it may become a site of corruption where companies and unions work together to manage the political impulses of low-paid precarious workers, a zombie revival of the company union of the 1920s. Company unions weren’t just anti-worker; they were anti-democracy. The corporatism — the integration of the state, big business, and the working class — that they embodied was part of an American fascist movement, similar to formations that took root in Benito Mussolini’s Italy at the same time. In the United States, company unions were made illegal by the NLRA. As the gig economy carves out exemptions for itself, it undoes the New Deal. Against a backdrop of increasing authoritarianism — with Silicon Valley a visible willing partner — labor’s consent to such terms is disappointing, if not chilling. Toward International Platform Worker Solidarity In our book Notes Toward a Digital Workers’ Inquiry , my collaborators and I highlight the struggles of self-organizing digital worker campaigns, many of whom are misclassified and denied full labor rights. Rather than approach this understanding from the perspective of the organizations cutting deals, we examine them from the perspective of workers themselves, in solidarity with their own organizing efforts. As a collaborative effort, digital workers’ inquiry can feed into labor organizing efforts within and against digital capitalism and help develop strategies for a more democratic labor movement. Independent worker organizing must continue globally. The International Association of App-Based Transport Workers, which was founded after RDU led the global strike against Uber’s IPO in 2019, has played a major role in pushing forward new standards for “decent work in the platform economy” adopted by the International Labor Organization (ILO). The convention calls for member states to “take measures to respect, promote and realize, in the platform economy, the fundamental principles and rights at work” including “freedom of association and the effective recognition of the right to collective bargaining.” In addition, states are “to ensure the correct classification of digital platform workers in respect of the existence or non-existence of an employment relationship.” While the United States opposed this, the convention was passed in a vote of 406–8. Gig workers have, over the course of the last decade, built their own organizations and through their collective activity changed the discourse about platform labor. By fighting their bosses, they have garnered media attention and won the ears of policymakers, making it clear that this is not a “sharing economy” or a way to “get your side hustle on” but a new model of exploitation that uses technology to target the most vulnerable workers. They have done this with minimal institutional backing, funding, and political support. The fight for gig workers to have their labor rights recognized has always been uphill. Guided by the principles outlined by the ILO, workers in the United States can play a role in supporting their siblings abroad, even as they face legal challenges and, potentially, hostility from bosses and some unions alike. We must make sense of the range of experiences that platform workers have from country to country, and to develop strategies that unite them across disparate experiences to demand justice. Platform labor’s fight has not been won, but neither is it over.

articles.title: The Left and Right Share a Moral Theory of Exploitation
articles.author: Benjamin Ferguson
articles.content: It is a truism that the Left and Right disagree about exploitation. For the Left, and Marxists in particular, exploitation offers the ultimate normative condemnation of capitalist markets. “Capital,” Karl Marx wrote , “is dead labor that, vampire-like, only lives by sucking living labor.” It is the exploitative extraction of workers’ labor, transformed into capital, that perpetuates the domination of the working classes. Libertarian philosopher Robert Nozick disagreed — to put it politely — arguing in Anarchy, State, and Utopia that because Marxists misunderstand the nature of price and value and ignore the contributions of capitalists, “Marxian exploitation is the exploitation of people’s lack of understanding of economics.” It would be hard to sketch a deeper ideological gulf. The Left and the Right appear to operate in completely different moral universes — a chasm that shouldn’t surprise anyone who has witnessed the polarization that has shaped our political discourse over the past two decades. Pundits insist that when it comes to the economy, there is no common ground. And yet our research finds that this picture is simply false, at least when it comes to exploitation. When asked what they think exploitation is, participants on both the Left and Right agree . And perhaps surprisingly, the pattern that emerges is one that vindicates the common claim of those on the Left that exploitation involves one party’s unjust use of power to gain at the expense of another. The results of our study provide a striking vindication of the Left’s structural critique of economic relations. And as we will argue, they suggest a way forward for the Left’s political strategy. Framing the Question Our study asked participants one simple question (followed of course by some demographic questions). We presented participants with a hypothetical scenario or vignette and asked, “Based only on the information provided, how exploitative is this scenario in your opinion?” Now, one challenge with this approach is that many real-world examples are too entangled with existing political biases, media narratives, and emotional reactions. If you ask whether workers in a Bangladeshi sweatshop producing trendy clothing are exploited, you will elicit predictably biased responses that align with the polarized views sketched above. Similar biases are manifest if you transparently ask about theorists’ definitions of exploitation — if you ask whether “the unequal exchange of labor is exploitation” — you will get a yes from those who accept the classic Marxist account and a no from everyone else. To eliminate various confounding factors, we constructed abstract vignettes that centered on a neutral, everyday economic activity: the production, purchase, or sale of mugs (because these are inexpensive, familiar, and morally neutral). We then pored over existing definitions of exploitation and identified common properties that different thinkers had identified as components of exploitation. These included: inequality , whether the economic gains from the transaction were split unevenly between the parties; power , whether one party held a strong structural advantage, such as being the only available employer; basic needs , whether the terms of the transaction left the weaker party in a position where their basic human needs were unmet; disrespect , whether the dominant party displayed a disrespectful attitude toward the weaker party; and luck , whether the weaker party’s vulnerability was the result of bad brute luck, like a natural disaster. We also included injustice , a property that further distinguished power by denoting that the power advantage was not merely accidental but rather the result of a prior injustice or rights violation. We tested all these properties in various combinations on two kinds of scenarios. Relational scenarios involved a direct transaction between two specific parties, while nonrelational scenarios described broader patterns of how wealth and resources are distributed across society. Finally, we developed two baseline cases that excluded any potentially exploitative factors: one relational and one nonrelational. In total, this gave us thirty-one clear vignettes to test. This modular design allowed us to isolate the exact impact, or “treatment effect,” of each distinct property on participants’ evaluations. Who were our participants? They included 551 professional academic philosophers recruited from top-rated global institutions and 1,546 members of the general public, split pretty much evenly between participants based in the United States (777) and the United Kingdom (769). The participants read through 10 vignettes, one at a time. They were first shown the two baseline vignettes and then eight more from the pool of 31. Here’s an example of a relational vignette that includes the properties of power, inequality, and injustice: B wants mugs and A is the only vendor selling mugs because other sellers have been unjustly excluded from the market. A sells mugs to B and the agreed price benefits A more than B. For each vignette, participants answered the same question: “Based only on the information provided, how exploitative is this scenario in your opinion?” They recorded their judgments using an active slider scale ranging from 0 (“not at all”) to 50 (“moderately”) up to 100 (“maximally”). One possible concern with this approach is that a score of 35 might mean different things to different participants. We address this concern by using “individual fixed effects” in our baseline empirical model, which allows us to control for constant but unobserved influences on individual evaluations, including differences in “exploitation anchors.” In practical terms, we estimate how much the presence of power, for example, changes the average reported score for each individual, and then calculate the average of these differences across all individuals. Importantly, the results are much the same when these fixed effects are excluded or observable characteristics are included instead. Assessing Exploitation So, what did we find? The results were rather surprising. It turns out that experts and members of the public order the properties associated with exploitation in nearly the same way. Neither group thought being relational/nonrelational or the presence of bad luck made much of a difference to exploitation. The scores for both were close to zero. Here’s a table showing the order and scores for the properties that made more of a difference for both participant pools, all of which are highly statistically significant. Property Experts General Public Injustice +28 +30 Asymmetric Power +21 +16 Inequality of Gains +16 +23 Unmet Basic Needs +13 +18 Disrespect +2 +12 As you can see, the two participant groups only differ in the relative importance they attach to inequality and power, with experts rating power over inequality and the public ranking them the other way around. And now to the result teased in the introduction: when we divided the two groups down by political orientation, the ordering of the properties was the same . Liberal and less liberal academics ranked the properties in the same order shown in the table. The same is true for more and less liberal members of the public. Further, we asked philosophers whether they identified as libertarians, communitarians, egalitarians, capitalists, or socialists. Again, the ordering was the same. At least on this issue, libertarians and capitalists agree with socialists and egalitarians: injustice, inequality, and power are the most significant drivers of exploitation. Now, it is important not to overstate the similarities between these groups. Participants’ sociopolitical orientation significantly impacted how much exploitation they saw. For example, libertarians’ scores were lower across the board. Compared to egalitarians they saw less exploitation in vignettes containing inequality (-10) and power (-15). Nevertheless, the fact that groups associated with the Left and Right gave the same orderings for the properties mean that both agree about what exploitation is . The lower scores from groups on the Right mean they are less likely to say that any particular scenario is exploitative. There’s one more result that’s worth emphasizing. While power alone, and inequality alone, move the needle for participants, the presence of both properties increases scores more than the sum of their individual effect. For example, for academics, vignettes containing only power raised scores by +14 and those with only inequality by +8, but when both appeared together scores increased by +34, which is 12 points greater than the sum of both alone. This “interaction premium” suggests that exploitation is more than the sum of its parts. This may be the study’s most important finding because it shows that the core of exploitation arises from a combination of factors. What triggers the strongest moral condemnation is the leverage of unequal power to engineer unequal outcomes. In other words, exploitation is recognized as effective bullying — the conversion of a structural power advantage into an unfair share of the economic pie. This result overturns two popular approaches to exploitation in the academic literature: purely distributive approaches, which take exploitation to merely be the maldistribution of gains, and purely power-based approaches, which argue that exploitation arises solely from the dominating use of power. What This Means for Contemporary Politics First, as we underscored in the introduction, our results reveal that exploitation is not an arbitrary or highly partisan invention. It is a stable, deeply embedded, and shared social concept. Across different classes, political outlooks, and educational backgrounds, people use a shared moral framework to evaluate exploitation: we look at the historical context, evaluate the balance of power, and measure the equity of the outcome. While agreement between the Left and Right on exploitation is surprising — especially given the contrasting views of Nozick and Marx presented above — perhaps it should not shock us altogether. After all, some of the populist right’s core anxieties arise from concerns about the cost of living, precarious employment, and the dominance of “big” industries (such as tech, pharma, and finance). And these overlap with perennial critiques from the political left. At their root, both the Left and Right are responding to the same structural reality: the deteriorating material conditions and economic vulnerability of large segments of the population. Second, the contemporary Left and Right — or at least their populist iterations — share another feature: a concern with political correctness, albeit in different forms. This concern is perhaps more charitably interpreted as a concern about esteem — or respect. While respect is an important moral value, an overemphasis on interpersonal attitudes and manners can shift the conversation away from hard structural metrics like wages and workplace power dynamics. To align with the current grievances, corporations pour resources into branding and public relations, changing their message to suit different markets. These attempts to humanize their operations by emphasizing themes of respect, inclusivity, and empathy in their corporate culture move the ethical conversation away from the material and power dynamics that really drive exploitation. Our study reveals a sharp divergence between experts and the public on the value of respect, shedding light on a feature of modern alienation. The disrespect variable had a negligible impact on academics’ scores (+2) — a polite boss, after all, extracts value just as effectively as a rude one. But for the general public, disrespect carried real weight (+12). This gap helps explain a crucial feature of our current political climate. Public discourse has focused on the increasing feelings of “alienation” and “loss of voice” of large segments of the population over the past few decades. One interpretation of our results is that this increased emphasis across the political spectrum means that for many working people, interpersonal disrespect is not just a breach of etiquette; it is the immediate, experiential manifestation of their structural vulnerability. It is how asymmetric power is lived and felt — whether on the shop floor, in the gig economy, or at the rental office. Organizing Around Power The agreement between the Left and Right — and indeed across many other demographic dimensions — that exploitation is the weaponization of unjust power to secure unequal outcomes suggests a path forward for the Left’s political agenda. It is clear that the public is fed up with the ideological defenses of low wages and bad options for work, housing, and health that appeal to the language of consumer choice and flexibility. If we want an economy free from exploitation that speaks to the material concerns that motivate populist politics on the Left and Right alike, then we must focus on policies that deliberately dismantle power asymmetries and protect vulnerable actors from being forced into desperate terms. That means increasing the power of vulnerable workers, which will require sectoral bargaining mandates to revitalize organized labor, increased minimum wages, and universal public housing and health care. And decreasing the power of the capitalist class, which will require wealth taxes and increased antitrust enforcement and regulation. When power is balanced, the capacity for one side to extract highly unequal, exploitative gains is dramatically curbed. Let us be clear. The message here is not that those on the Left should moderate their policies in the name of bipartisan harmony. The view of exploitation that emerges from our study is not that the truth lies somewhere between Marx and Nozick. Rather, the headline is that those on the Left and Right agree on a view of exploitation that is located much closer to Marx’s view, one that emphasizes the use of power accumulated through injustice to extract unequal gains. The interpretation of these results that we want to stress is that they represent an opportunity for the Left. They provide further evidence that the motivations of many populist views across the political spectrum are in fact compatible with historically leftist positions on power and equality. While contemporary headlines remain dominated by the culture wars, they frequently mask these deep-seated economic anxieties. The corporate preoccupation with etiquette and notions of respect that are not linked to power operates as a tempting distraction — one to which both the Right and Left are susceptible — from workers’ own anti-capitalist intuitions. Our study shows that a structural understanding of exploitation is not a niche theoretical framework but a commonsense shared reality. Rather than playing defense on the terms set by corporate public relations, the Left has a distinct opportunity to reanchor the political conversation around shared material interests and policies that dismantle the very power asymmetries that the public already condemns.
