articles.title: Yemen’s Ansar Allah escalates retaliatory attacks on Saudi interests
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Weeks after Saudi Arabia joined the US-Israeli war on the West Asia region with strikes on Yemen , Ansar Allah retaliated with intensified attacks on vital Saudi interests. This included targeting economic facilities inside Saudi Arabia, on Yemeni soil, and in the Red Sea, inflicting considerable losses on Riyadh. On Wednesday, August 5, the spokesperson of the Ansar Allah-led Yemeni Armed Forces, Brigadier General Yahya Sare’e, announced that the Saudi-flagged oil tanker NCC Wafaa was targeted with a number of ballistic missiles in the northern Red Sea, off the coast of Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu Port. Sare’e explained that the attack was launched as part of a maritime blockade, which the Yemeni movement has imposed on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea since July 22, in response to a decade-long comprehensive blockade imposed by Riyadh on Yemen. He further clarified that Wafaa was the eighth Saudi oil tanker targeted by Ansar Allah since the blockade started three weeks ago. Meanwhile, 29 other Saudi oil tankers and related ships were forced to turn back or change their route in the Red and Arabian Seas. “After the Yemeni Armed Forces succeeded in tightening the maritime blockade against the Saudi enemy through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the southern Red Sea, Saudi Arabia diverted the route of its oil tankers to the northern Red Sea. Therefore, the Yemeni Armed Forces confirms that its operations will continue and escalate to target Saudi vessels in the northern Red Sea in order to block all maritime access routes and prevent their passage. In this way, we implement a blockade for blockade equation,” Sare’e added. In another statement aired on Friday, August 7, Sare’e revealed the details of what he described as a “qualitative military operation” carried out against Saudi forces and allied fighters at the Sahn al-Jinn camp in Marib, in north-central Yemen. He said that the concentrations of these forces and fighters were targeted with a large number of missiles and drones after their movements were closely monitored. Weapons depots, vehicles, and military equipment were also struck in the attack. On Sunday, August 9, Sare’e announced that the Yemeni Armed Forces struck a refinery belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco in the coastal city of Jizan, in southwestern Saudi Arabia by a drone. The Yemeni spokesperson said that the operation was carried out in response to Saudi drone violations of Yemen’s sovereignty. That same day, Ansar Allah attacked Saudi military concentrations, reinforcements, and weapons depots in the Al-Mokha area with a large barrage of missiles and drones. The operation resulted in the destruction of military equipment, and left dozens of personnel, including Saudi nationals, killed or wounded, according to the Yemeni Armed Forces. Ansar Allah’s operations against Saudi troops, their weapons warehouses and command centers continued on Tuesday, August 11, and Wednesday, August 12, in Yemen’s Marib and Taiz provinces. Analysts estimate that the tension between Yemen’s Ansar Allah and Saudi Arabia will further escalate in the upcoming weeks, especially when Riyadh figures out that the traffic of its vessels was completely paralyzed, with the Strait of Hormuz also being closed until further notice. articles.title: Gaza Tribunal Co-Chairs MP Jeremy Corbyn, Neve Gordon & Shahd Hammouri on U.K. Complicity in Genocide
articles.content: From London, we revisit the Gaza Tribunal, an independent, nongovernmental inquiry into the United Kingdom’s complicity in the Israeli genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. The tribunal, held nearly one year ago, was chaired by our three guests: former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn, Israeli professor of human rights law Neve Gordon and Palestinian legal scholar Shahd Hammouri. Their new book is titled The Gaza Tribunal: Britain’s Complicity in Genocide . We discuss the recent apology from Prime Minister Andy Burnham over the Labour Party’s early support for Israel’s assault on Gaza, the United Kingdom’s crackdown on the Palestine Action protest group under counterterrorism laws, and whether British policymakers will face any accountability for participating in “one of the biggest crimes in humanity.”

articles.title: DRC, M23 begin exchange of 15 prisoners under Doha peace process
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 coalition have begun implementing a detainee-release arrangement agreed under the Doha peace process, with 15 people released and handed over to the armed group in eastern Congo. The operation, facilitated by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), took place between August 6 and 7, 2026. It’s one of the first tangible steps towards implementing commitments reached by the two sides during negotiations. According to the ICRC , the 15 detainees, who had consented to taking part in the operation, left Beni in North Kivu in a convoy on the evening of August 6. The convoy traveled through Uganda, which had agreed to facilitate their passage, before arriving in Rutshuru Territory in southern North Kivu on August 7. The detainees were subsequently handed over to the AFC/M23. ICRC calls for further releases “We hope that this operation will bring some comfort to families who have been separated for so long from their loved ones,” said Stephanie Eller, head of operations for the ICRC in Kinshasa. Saying the operation could pave the way for further detainee releases agreed upon by the parties during their negotiations. Under the Doha process, the ICRC says it is acting exclusively as a neutral intermediary at the request of the parties, particularly in facilitating the safe transportation and handover of people released by them. The ICRC has also stressed that its role remains strictly humanitarian. Under international humanitarian law, detainees must be treated humanely under all circumstances, while their safety must be ensured during release operations. Doha agreements yet to be fully implemented The current process follows a series of agreements reached through the Doha negotiations. The framework began with a Declaration of Principles signed on July 19, 2025, followed by an agreement establishing a prisoner-exchange mechanism on September 14 and a ceasefire monitoring and verification mechanism on October 14. Read more: DRC–Rwanda leaders head to Washington for final peace deal with Trump However, the release of the 15 detainees is being viewed cautiously by Congolese in eastern Congo. ‘A confidence-building measure’ Speaking to BreakThrough News , LUCHA member Stewart Muhindo described the transfer as an important but limited development. “The two stakeholders agreed to release the prisoners from both sides. Almost one year after that agreement, now we can see the first signs of that agreement,” Muhindo said, adding that the development was being received positively by communities affected by the conflict. Muhindo nevertheless described the operation primarily as a confidence-building measure rather than evidence that the broader peace process was advancing smoothly. He pointed to the nearly one-year gap between the agreement and its first implementation, as well as the limited number of detainees involved, as indications of the difficulties facing the process. The agreement envisaged the release of larger numbers of detainees, Muhindo said, while noting that so far only one side had carried out a release. “We still need to see if the M23 side will also respect its commitments,” he said. Ceasefire remains a major test The detainee exchange also comes amid continuing concerns over the implementation of other elements of the Doha framework, including the ceasefire and broader security arrangements. For Muhindo, the main challenge is that both the Congolese government and M23 have interests that could make implementation difficult. “The Congolese government is trying to use the war to advance its project of changing the Constitution and allowing President Félix Tshisekedi to remain in power. The M23, meanwhile, is gaining economic benefits from mining and continues to receive support from Rwanda. If peace is achieved, the M23 could lose much of its current position and influence. As a result, both parties to the Doha agreement have interests that could encourage the continuation of the conflict. Read more: Lithium mining in the DRC: A new mineral rush spearheaded by the US, EU, and other major powers That is the most difficult situation we are facing now, because it is the civilian population that continues to suffer from the war, while these two stakeholders are gaining from it,” Muhindo said. If the operation leads to further detainee exchanges and progress on the wider ceasefire commitments will depend on the willingness of both parties to implement the remaining provisions of the agreement. This is the first step among many, and it remains to be seen whether it can be sustained, particularly as part of efforts to achieve long-term peace agreement.

articles.title: 21st-century McCarthyism: Cuba in the crosshairs
articles.author: Guillermo R Barreto
articles.content: It happened on May 25, 2020, in Minneapolis, in the US. George Floyd (a Black man) was arrested on suspicion of attempting to pay for a pack of cigarettes with a counterfeit $20 bill. Police officer Derek Chauvin (a white man) pinned him to the ground and pressed down on his neck for more than 9 minutes. It was to no avail that George Floyd repeated “I can’t breathe” more than 20 times. He lost consciousness and died of asphyxiation. In other words, he was murdered by the police officer. This incident sparked a wave of outrage and protests that spread to more than 2,000 cities across the US and beyond. US history reveals a long record of discriminatory policies that reflect a structurally racist system. Outrage over the ruthless murder of a Black man at the hands of a white police officer seems like an inevitable reaction. Despite this, the US State Department has found no better explanation than to attribute responsibility for the protests to the Cuban government, whose “founding myth and central principle is to wipe the US off the face of the Earth,” as stated in an infamous report published on July 20, 2026, titled “ Cuba. The Capital of 21st-Century Communism .” The State Department report, which appears to have been generated by artificial intelligence, is a collection of clichés reminiscent of the era of Republican Senator Joseph McCarthy, who launched an anti-communist crusade between 1950 and 1954 that led to the persecution, dismissal, or imprisonment of anyone accused of belonging to or sympathizing with leftist movements – actions interpreted as “anti-American activities.” In general, there was never a judicial investigation linking the accused to such activities. A committee was created that summoned the accused, who were required to denounce acquaintances with alleged leftist views. The harassment reached such a level that refusing to answer by invoking the constitutional right against self-incrimination (Fifth Amendment) was considered proof of guilt. Now, in the middle of 2026, the State Department is appealing to fear to create a fantasy that portrays the Cuban government and its intelligence services as the greatest threat facing the world’s greatest military power, thereby generating a climate of paranoia among the US population that fuels mistrust and sets the stage for a possible armed attack on the island. In that report, Cuba is accused of having supported resistance movements against dictatorial and criminal regimes such as the Tupamaros, who fought against the Uruguayan dictatorship in the 1970s, the Sandinista Front, which overthrew the Somoza dictatorship in Nicaragua, or the Venezuelan guerrillas of the 1960s, who fought against the social democratic governments of Betancourt and Leoni – regimes that practiced and perfected forced disappearances, torture, and extrajudicial executions. Although the report, just as McCarthy did, presents no evidence against Cuba, there is at least no doubt that the accusation is based on Cuba’s support for those who resisted criminal governments that have been heavily criticized by history. It seems that the AI used failed to notice this detail. The 99-page report lists the numerous actions that, without any evidence, the Cuban government allegedly carries out to infiltrate not only the US government but also social movements, labor unions, universities, and scientific and cultural platforms. It is a narrative that mixes a few verified convictions for espionage with unverified testimonies from defectors or reports from Congress, the CIA, or the FBI that cannot be substantiated. What the report omits are the more than 60 years of U.S. aggression against Cuba, including the illegal blockade – which has been repeatedly condemned each year by the United Nations General Assembly and has caused cumulative damages since its inception amounting to $ 164 billion dollars – armed attacks such as the Bay of Pigs invasion, the more than 600 assassination attempts against Commander-in-Chief Fidel Castro, and the bombing of Cubana de Aviación Flight 455 on October 6, 1976 – which killed 73 people and whose masterminds, Orlando Bosch and Luis Posada Carriles, lived under the protection of the United States until their deaths. The State Department uses this report to incriminate all forms of dissent within the US, conflating different eras and movements (such as the Black Panthers, Black Lives Matter, lawyers’ associations, universities, and solidarity brigades) as part of an alleged plan to destroy “American values.” Suddenly, it turns out that academic agreements between the University of Havana and US universities are part of an espionage agenda, that Cuba’s tourism development plans are part of an indoctrination agenda, and that the Cuban medical brigade is actually a brigade of spies scattered around the world to destroy Western values. The State Department report (now headed by Marco Rubio, a liar, opportunist, and ambitious politician) has no academic or intelligence value. That is not its significance. Its significance lies in the fact that it explicitly reveals an essentially fascist government that seeks to impose itself on the world through force, censorship, and fear – and this includes the American people themselves. The Argentine writer Julio Cortázar wrote: “To be a fascist – even if no one has defined it exactly – one need only observe it as a form of behavior to sense that its root is negative, that it stems from fear.” It is precisely that fear that the Trump administration uses to justify its authoritarian actions. The evil enemy is first called a communist, then a terrorist, an Islamist, a drug trafficker, a migrant, and now, once again, a communist. A dangerous course of action that seeks to build an international platform of repression in the style of a renewed and reinforced Operation Condor, using sophisticated technological tools to ruthlessly attack Cuba – but which aims to destroy anything that challenges it. This year we commemorate the centennial of Commander-in-Chief Fidel Castro. Like few others, Fidel embodies human dignity and the defense of principles as unyielding values for building that other possible and necessary world of justice, equality, and peace. Where Cuba sends medical brigades, the United States sends soldiers trained to kill. Where Cuba sends teachers to teach reading and writing and bring light to marginalized communities, the United States sends media trash, alienation, darkness, and death. Cuba has withstood humanity’s greatest threat with dignity, and it is the duty of all of us to voice our strongest condemnation of the policies implemented by the US government (as outlined in that despicable report today) and to express our solidarity, on the centennial of Commander Fidel Castro, with that brave people. Guillermo R. Barreto is Venezuelan and holds a Ph.D. in Science (University of Oxford). He is a retired professor at Simón Bolívar University (Venezuela). He served as Deputy Minister of Science and Technology, President of the National Fund for Science and Technology, and Minister of Ecosocialism and Water (Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela). He is currently a researcher at the Tricontinental Institute for Social Research and a visiting scholar at the Center for the Study of Social Transformations-IVIC. articles.title: Hundreds of thousands in India protest proposed trade agreement with the US
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Hundreds of thousands of people marched on the streets across India, with thousands risking arrest in various parts of the country on Monday, August 10. The actions were part of a joint national call by peasant and worker unions opposing the proposed trade agreement with the US and raising other demands. The protesters, which included farmers, informal and formal sector workers, students, youth and women, marched in several cities and towns in India to their respective government offices carrying banners and red flags, and raising slogans of peasant-worker unity against government policies. At some places they also clashed with the security forces trying to block their marches and laid a temporary siege of the government offices. The protesters demanded the withdrawal of the proposed Indo-US trade deal announced by the Donald Trump administration earlier this year, calling it antithetical to Indian agriculture. They published a detailed charter of the demand as well. At various places large gatherings were organized where speakers reminded the audience of the failures of the Narendra Modi government in fulfilling major promises related to the welfare of the country’s farmers. The speakers talked about how a series of legislation brought by this government has actually harmed the interests of the farmers and the country’s rural economy, which has long been in distress. The speakers accused that by supporting a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with the US, the ultra-right-wing government, led by the Hindu-supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), has yet again exposed its subordination to imperialist dictates and its indifference to the country’s real interests. A large number of protesters were seen on the streets of various Indian states, such as West Bengal , Kerala , Tamilnadu , Tripura, Rajasthan , Haryana , Assam, Maharashtra, among others. The protest was jointly called by Samyukta Kisan Morcha (SKM) and Central Trade Unions (CTUs) along with the All India Agricultural Workers Association (AIAWA) and was supported by students, youth, and women’s unions. SKM has issued a charter of demands and given the government until November 26, the sixth anniversary of the farmers agitation on the borders of Delhi, to fulfill those demands, warning of a larger indefinite movement otherwise. Agricultural distress in India under Modi The SKM and CTUs, representing millions of farmers and workers, have claimed the November 26 protests would be their joint attempt to “Save Agriculture, Save Industry and Save India.” More than 40% of India’s workforce and nearly 60% of its population is still dependent on agriculture and related fields for their livelihood. Around 70% of Indians still live in rural areas. Decades of neoliberal economic reforms have negatively impacted the rural economy and agriculture, causing massive agricultural distress with hundreds of thousands farmers committing suicide due to indebtness and the lack of an alternative means of living. The distress has forced millions to abandon agriculture and migrate to cities seeking alternative sources of livelihood. Instead of addressing their issues, the Modi government which came to power in 2014, farmers accuse, has adopted policies which have further harmed their interests. This has led to several rounds of mass protests in the last decade. After over a year-long farmer protest at the borders of the capital, New Delhi, the Modi government was forced to sign an agreement with the SKM on December 9, 2021 . It agreed to withdraw contentious agricultural laws it had brought in 2019 and to enact a law for the legal Minimum Support Price (MSP) for agricultural products to address a long standing demand of farmers. The SKM claims that, due to the absence of a legal MSP, farmers are often forced to sell their products at prices much lower than their actual cost of production, incurring huge financial losses every season. However, five years later, farmers are alleging that none of the demands which the Modi government agreed to were fulfilled. “The Narendra Modi government has failed to fulfill its promises of implementing a legal MSP and withdrawing cases against the protesters made during the farmers agitation five years ago,” Hannan Mollah, one of the leaders of the 2020-21 farmers agitation and leader of the All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS), a major constituent of the SKM, said in a message. He accused the Modi government of enacting more policies which make the lives of farmers and workers in the country even more difficult. The government has introduced more contentious legislation, including a bill for the privatization of electricity and the withdrawal of the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA) , a major relief for millions of peasants looking for some work during the period between two crops and signed several FTAs with countries like New Zealand, EU, and the UK. Major demands The proposed trade deal with the US has caused concern among millions of farmers about the possible tariff-free imports of American agricultural products. The tariff-free entry of highly subsidized agricultural products from the US and other countries will make Indian agricultural products even more expensive for local consumers, the SKM claims. This will displace millions more from farming with no alternative means of living. Apart from the withdrawal of all FTAs and the proposed trade deal with the US, there are six other major demands raised by the protesters; An MSP law on the basis of C2+50% (total cost of production+50% profit) for all agricultural products A comprehensive loan waiver to end rural indebtedness address suicides of peasants and daily wagers’ The withdrawal of four labor codes and a national minimum wage of Rs. 31,000 (around $325 per month) The restoration of the NREGA and a minimum 200 days of guaranteed work for all The withdrawal of the electricity privatization bill An end to all forceful land acquisitions AIKS, in a press release on Saturday, had called the protests a message to the government about the strong peasant-workers unity against “the brutal exploitation of farmers and workers by the corporate capitalist forces through the denial of minimum support price to farmers and minimum wage for a dignified life to workers and agricultural workers.” The SKM and CTUs have been working in tandem for months now mobilizing against the anti-worker and anti-farmer policies of the Modi government. SKM had supported the national strike against the four new labor codes on February 12 in which an estimated 300 million Indians participated. Read more: Anatomy of a general strike: how workers in the Indian state of Karnataka shut down production SKM has warned that if the government fails to listen to the farmers and workers after the protests on Monday it will send a mass delegation to the prime minister of India on August 17 to submit the charter of its demands and begin preparing for the indefinite protests from November 26 by carrying out local level campaigns.

articles.title: Anas al-Sharif: the voice of truth Israel failed to defeat
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: August 10 marks the first anniversary of the assassination of prominent Palestinian journalist Anas al-Sharif. Al-Sharif, alongside five other Palestinian journalists, was killed on August 10, 2025, when Israeli warplanes targeted their tent near Al-Shifa Hospital in Western Gaza city. Israel claimed that the six slain journalists were combatants affiliated with Palestinian resistance groups. A pretext that it has long used to justify killings of journalists. Al-Sharif was exceptional in documenting one of the most cruel genocides in modern history, driven by his unparalleled devotion to his people, his dedication to delivering the truth, his steadfastness and defiance, despite repeated threats of assassination by Israel. Working in the most dangerous war zones for journalists in the world, Anas did not surrender even after his father was killed in an Israeli airstrike that also demolished his family’s house. Nor did the prolonged starvation defeat his determination. “I have lived through pain in all its details, tasted suffering and loss many times, yet I never once hesitated to convey the truth as it is, without distortion or falsification,” Anas wrote in his last will. Anas al-Sharif: the iconic journalist Anas al-Sharif, a father of two, became an icon not only because of his professional journalistic work and unmatched bravery, but also because of the deeply human moments captured on camera, showing him weeping over the suffering of his people. Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails, such as the prominent Dr. Abu Safiya, cut off from the outside world and unaware of al-Sharif’s assassination, sent pleas to the late journalist asking him “to remind the world about our cause and our suffering.” Anas al-Sharif was one of over 270 Palestinian journalists killed by Israel in less than three years. This happened in full view of the international community, and with unwavering US support for the Israeli war machine. WATCH: Israel Killed Shireen. The U.S. Covered It Up. Now Journalists Are Being Hunted Israel also killed dozens of other journalists across the West Asia region over the same period, including in Lebanon , Yemen , and Iran . Although Israeli fighter jets ended Anas al-Sharif’s life, they could not silence his voice, which has inspired many journalists to follow his path and continue to speak up fearlessly for their people.

articles.title: Where is the left? Jordanian communist leader reflects on the challenges facing the progressive camp
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: ​Following major geopolitical shifts in West Asia, a question has been raised frequently: where is the left and why has it been unable to defeat capitalism and imperialism? BreakThrough News spoke with Dr. Emad Al-Hatabeh, a central committee member of the Jordanian Communist Party, for his insights into the state of contemporary left movements in the world, and those in the Arab region in particular. There is no monolithic left, says Al-Hatabeh Dr. Emad Al-Hatabeh argues that the left is not in a crisis, but the very concept of “the left” as it is understood today is the crisis. This resulted from the broad categorization of the “left,” which contains severe ideological and practical contradictions within a label that attempts to encompass both Western social democrats and Third World liberation movements. According to the Jordanian communist leader, the umbrella of “the left” ranges from reformist Western politicians like Bernie Sanders, Jeremy Corbyn, and Zohran Mamdani to armed Maoist guerrillas in the jungles of the Philippines. “The fragmentation of left thought across an excessively wide ideological spectrum has weakened its core identity. This in turn makes a unified political position nearly impossible to identify,” Dr. Emad affirmed. Read more: Resisting the upcoming US campaign in West Asia Reform vs. revolution Dr. Emad clarified the contradiction between the left in Western countries, and those in the Global South in terms of their position in relation to capitalism. “Western left movements largely seek to reform and humanize capitalism from within liberal democratic frameworks. Yet, radical liberation movements, which represent the left in the Global South, seek the systemic overthrow of imperialism and capitalism,” he said. This contradiction has also extended to include the definition of the working class. “The traditional working class has also been fragmented and affected by capitalist and imperial factors. A worker in the West benefits economically from a military facility within the global defense industrial complex, which manufactures weapons used against agrarian workers in the Global South,” Dr. Emad noted. Furthermore, he highlighted that some left movements have tended toward pragmatism, fearing state repression due to the demonization of communists in the post-Soviet era. ​Consequently, many left parties have abandoned revolutionary theory in favor of “minimum-baseline” reforms. These parties operate entirely within bourgeois electoral frameworks, chasing the illusion of achieving socialist transformation through capitalist democratic mechanisms. Al-Hatabeh slammed some left parties for receiving Western NGO funding, stressing that anti-imperialist movements cannot oppose imperialism while surviving on its money. “These acts erode the left’s credibility among the public,” he asserted. Contemporary challenges facing the left ​Dr. Emad contends that while local context dictates tactical positions – such as responses to military coups or domestic governance – the identity of the left must remain uncompromising on key structural issues, including private property, capitalism, and imperialism. “There should be a distinction between personal and private property within the modern Marxist framework,” Al-Hattabeh maintained. “While extremist interpretations often call for the total abolition of property, personal property, such as a person’s home, car, or small family business is not what leftist ideology targets,” he explained. “Private property, in a Marxist sense, must be defined as asset ownership leveraged to exploit labor and generate surplus value,” Dr. Emad continues. The crisis of the Arab left When it comes to the Arab left, Dr. Emad sees that it has historically faced a deep structural issue. “Leftist ideology in the Arab region was largely imported by intellectuals, who were abroad and returned to their countries bringing that ideology with them,” he said. Dr. Emad also indicated that left groups in the Arab world historically emerged from splits within nationalist and petty-bourgeois movements rather than grassroots labor struggles. As a result, many remain disconnected from the daily realities of working-class communities and rural populations. He believes that anti-capitalist struggles do not fully apply to the Arab world, as its countries are not heavily industrialized and operate on the edges of the global capitalist system rather than at its core. They are dominated by comprador elites and brokers rather than productive industrial capital. ​”We fought non-existent domestic industrial capitalists with slogans designed for European economies,” Dr. Emad remarked, referencing the analysis of Lebanese theorist Mahdi Amel. Instead, the region’s primary historical tether to leftist ideology has been anti-imperialism, forged during decades of 20th-century colonial rule. Read more: Reflections on the US-Israeli multi-front war in West Asia: How the Axis of Resistance remains resilient How could the left overcome the crisis? Dr. Emad suggests that Marxism and socialist theory must function as an adaptable, evolving science for working-class struggle rather than a fixed set of tenets, so that they remain relevant to modern realities. “Modern analysis must transcend the typical 19th-century imagery of factory workers in overalls. Today’s working class includes tech workers, service employees, and any individual forced to sell mental or physical labor to generate surplus value for capital,” he said. “The foundational identity of the left must remain uncompromised by completely ending human exploitation,” he added. Dr. Emad pointed out that offering a genuine alternative to global capitalism entails a clear structural breakdown of class interests, an embrace of transformative principles, and a rejection of reformist pragmatism. According to Dr. Emad, if the left – both globally and within the Arab region – hopes to regain efficacy, it cannot rely on single-issue politics. It must instead comprehensively integrate its core principles into every action and political stance. This includes confronting imperialism and fascism, challenging capitalism, advancing class struggle, championing social progress, advocating for wealth redistribution, and clearly addressing the dynamics of private and personal property.

articles.title: Maternal mortality doubled in the Ebola epicenter in DRC
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: Maternal deaths have nearly doubled in Ituri province, epicenter of the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak ever recorded, ravaging the northeastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). About six women are “dying each week from childbirth-related complications,” Farhan Haq, deputy spokesperson for the UN secretary-general, said in a press conference on August 7. ​ Fear of catching the disease in healthcare facilities, “combined with disruptions to services,” is keeping people from seeking medical care, said John Agbor, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Representative in the DRC.​ “Ebola infection during pregnancy remains associated with almost universal fetal loss,” added Haq.​ However, as women avoid healthcare facilities fearing infection, childbirth without medical supervision is on the rise, as indicated by a 13% fall in deliveries at healthcare facilities across the province since the outbreak was declared on May 15​. According to UNICEF, the percentage drop is far higher in the hotspots within Ituri: 30% in Rwampara, 38% in Bunia, and a steep 70% in Nizi. This drop in facility-assisted deliveries correlates with the near doubling of maternal mortality.​ Children are also at high risk, as the routine administration of vaccine shots has halved in the hotspots. This compounds the dangers the “children already face directly from Ebola itself,” UNICEF said in a statement , adding that although less than a quarter of the confirmed cases have been detected in children, they account for a third of all the deaths. The case fatality rate is almost double that of adults in children below the age of five. Over 60% of the infected children in this age group have died.​ In less than three months since the outbreak was declared on May 15, the disease has killed at least 1,850 and infected more than 4,000 people as of August 5, in what has become the largest ever Ebola outbreak recorded in DRC. The speed of its spread is outpacing the West Africa outbreak in 2014, which killed 11,325 and infected 28,600 across many countries. However, in the first three months since the outbreak was declared, it had infected 759 and killed 467 – a fraction of the number of confirmed cases and deaths in the current outbreak, which had spread over 51 health zones across five provinces. All of them are located in the conflict-ridden northeast of the country, including the provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu, large portions of which are occupied by the Rwandan military and its proxy, the M23 armed group. This has imposed additional difficulty in tracing and responding to the health emergency.

articles.title: World Breastfeeding Week 2026: ‘Cost of not breastfeeding borne by families, health systems’
articles.author: Peoples Health Dispatch
articles.content: “Across the world, millions of families who want to breastfeed cannot, not because of a lack of will, but because the systems around them fall short,” the World Alliance for Breastfeeding Action (WABA) wrote ahead of World Breastfeeding Week , marked August 1-7. Despite widespread recognition of breastfeeding’s health benefits for both children and women, many countries still struggle to support it. Industry lobbying and limited labor protections persist as significant barriers. Since 2020, exclusive breastfeeding rates for babies under six months have risen by 8 percentage points to 47% globally. However, other indicators, such as early initiation of breastfeeding, have moved in the opposite direction, WABA emphasized. These fluctuations should signal to governments that investments in breastfeeding measures and metrics must be ramped up. “The cost of not breastfeeding is borne by families, health systems and national economies alike,” WABA pointed out. Read more: Childbirth under capitalism Strengthening health systems is a crucial part of the solution. This means adequate staffing of midwives, nurses, and community health workers to support families in initiating breastfeeding must be secured, while also respecting maternity leave recommendations. “A systematic review of 35 studies from low- and middle-income countries found that paid maternity leave was associated with a 52% increase in exclusive breastfeeding,” the World Health Organization (WHO) noted. The International Labor Organization (ILO) sets the baseline at 14 weeks of maternity leave , while the Global Breastfeeding Collective , echoing additional resolutions by the global labor agency, calls for countries to “mandate paid maternity leave for a minimum of 18 weeks, and preferably for a period of six months or more after birth.” Yet according to WABA, only 10% of countries worldwide meet ILO standards on this, with others falling behind on elements like guaranteed remuneration and duration. This is not exclusive to low-income countries. Famously, the United States has no federal provisions that meet basic ILO criteria for paid maternity leave. And despite breastfeeding promotion appearing on the second Trump administration’s health priorities list, food and nutrition experts recently noted no action has been taken. “Stronger laws are also urgently needed to restrict the marketing of breastmilk substitutes, including digital marketing , to ensure full compliance,” the Global Breastfeeding Collective stated in its 2025 scorecard . “ Formula companies continue to exploit loopholes and engage in tactics that undermine global efforts to protect infant nutrition, health and development.” Read more: Intergenerational hunger: the effects of Israel’s starvation of Gaza Beyond investment in public health systems and effective regulation, networks participating in World Breastfeeding Week 2026 also warned of the impact conflicts and crises have on breastfeeding practices. International agencies have called for dedicated emergency response policies to be included in broader breastfeeding promotion plans. Conditions in Gaza serve as a dire warning. At the end of July, Save the Children warned that obstructions to supply deliveries enforced by the Israeli occupation are – still – having a devastating impact on women and children’s health. “Some mothers are resorting to feeding their children water mixed with ground chickpeas or tahini, while others are stopping breastfeeding earlier than they would prefer, due to difficulties and lack of support,” the organization wrote. “UN data from July 2026 shows that of the nearly 29,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women screened for malnutrition, more than 20,000 – or two of three – require targeted supplementary feeding.” “In emergency situations like Gaza, infants who are not breastfed face significantly higher risks of illness and dehydration, malnutrition, and death,” Save the Children emphasized. articles.title: Paul Biya’s absence raises concerns over leadership in Cameroon
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Cameroon’s 93-year-old President Paul Biya is facing scrutiny over his prolonged absence from the country, with growing questions about his whereabouts, health, and the continuity of government. Biya has not been publicly seen in Cameroon since June 7, when he left the country for what authorities described as a short private stay in Europe. More than two months later, he remains abroad, with his prolonged absence fueling speculation among opposition figures and sections of the public about the state of his health and the extent to which he is directing the government from outside the country. Read more: At 92, Paul Biya declares eighth presidential bid to lead Cameroon The government has rejected suggestions that the country is facing a leadership vacuum. In an interview with RFI , communications minister and government spokesperson René Emmanuel Sadi said Biya was alive, had not resigned and would return to Cameroon soon. He also dismissed reports that the president was hospitalized in Geneva, saying there were no grounds to speak of a vacancy at the head of state. The government has not, however, provided a specific date for Biya’s return. The latest concern is not unprecedented. Biya has frequently spent extended periods outside Cameroon, particularly in Switzerland and France, and his long stays abroad have previously generated questions about his health and the way the country is governed. In 2024, similar speculation intensified after he was absent from public view for several weeks. Government officials at the time also moved to reassure the public that he was alive and working from Geneva. What makes the current absence particularly concerning is the timing. Biya has just begun another seven-year presidential term after being sworn in for an eighth term in November 2025. He has ruled Cameroon since 1982 and is the world’s oldest serving head of state. Military reshuffle from abroad While concerns over his absence have grown, presidential powers continue to be exercised. In early August , presidential decrees announced a major reshuffle of Cameroon’s military leadership. The measures included the promotion of some of the colonels to brigadier general, as well as changes to commanders in four of the country’s five joint military regions. The reshuffle has attracted particular attention because of the central role of the security forces in maintaining political stability in Cameroon. The decrees have not been accompanied by an official explanation linking the military changes to Biya’s absence. Analysts have nevertheless interpreted the timing as evidence that the president remains focused on maintaining control over the country’s core political and security structures even while abroad. Read more: Is Cameroon’s presidency headed for a dynastic succession? Biya has also continued to sign government decisions from outside the country, including financial and administrative measures, reinforcing the government’s position that the president remains actively engaged in state affairs. Opposition demands clarity Due to the long absence, opposition parties have intensified calls for greater transparency over the president’s condition and the functioning of the state. The debate became particularly pronounced in July, when opposition figures questioned whether Cameroon could continue to operate normally without the president being physically present in the country. The Social Democratic Front described the country as being on “autopilot,” while the Union for Democracy in Cameroon called for institutional mechanisms to deal with prolonged presidential absences and establish procedures for determining whether a president is temporarily or permanently unable to govern. The opposition has also questioned the implications of the constitutional changes adopted earlier this year. In April, Cameroon’s parliament approved an amendment reintroducing the position of vice president. The amendment was presented by the government as a mechanism to ensure continuity if the president dies, resigns or becomes incapacitated. The vice president would automatically assume the presidency in such circumstances. But no vice president has been appointed, leaving the newly created position vacant as Biya remains outside the country. Further the succession process of the vice president is appointed and can be dismissed by the head of state. At 93, Biya’s age has inevitably made questions about succession more prominent. His government has sought to counter those concerns by demonstrating that decisions continue to be issued in his name, while many argue that the public deserves greater clarity about who is exercising executive authority when the president is away for such an extended period. For now, the government insists that he remains in charge and will return. But as his absence stretches into its third month, questions persist.

articles.title: Bryan Stevenson on the “Enduring Evil of Slavery” and Trump’s Attempt to Rewrite History
articles.content: We spend the hour with civil rights lawyer Bryan Stevenson, founder and executive director of the Equal Justice Initiative. In 2018, the organization opened the Legacy Museum in Montgomery, Alabama, to tell the history of millions of enslaved Africans who were abducted and trafficked across the Atlantic to the Americas by European powers, and to chronicle the legacy of slavery, racism, lynchings and segregation in the United States. The Legacy Museum has just opened its first international exhibition as part of the Edinburgh International Festival in Scotland. “In putting together the content we have at the Legacy Museum, you begin to appreciate just how global the institution of slavery was,” Stevenson tells Democracy Now! host Amy Goodman in Edinburgh. “We were eager to have an opportunity to present this content on this continent, which … hasn’t done very much to acknowledge this history.” Stevenson details the Equal Justice Initiative’s goal of educating the public about racial iniquities, as well as his own family’s connection to slavery. “My foreparents did not come to this country seeking greater opportunity. They did not come seeking shelter from some distant threat. They came in chains. They were victims of a brutal abduction,” he says.
